Yossarian, an American bombardier on a speck of island near the war's end, has worked out that the people most determined to kill him are not the Germans but his own commanders, who keep raising the number of missions each time he nears the total that would send him home. Heller spins this single paradox outward into a whole circus, a mess officer bombing his own base under contract, a colonel in love with tidy formations, men vanishing into paperwork. And then the laughter, which has been frantic, almost cruel, turns out to have been guarding something. The novel keeps returning to a wounded gunner in the back of a plane, withholding the worst of it, until it can bear to tell you everything. You will not stop laughing, and you will not be ready.

title: The Windhover
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
extract: I caught this morning morning's minion, kingdom of daylight's dauphin, dapple-dawn-drawn Falcon
blurb: Watch a kestrel pin itself against a strong wind, wings beating to hold one point of sky perfectly still, and you have the thing Hopkins caught one morning in the Welsh hills and turned into the sonnet he called the best he ever wrote. The poem does not describe the bird so much as enact it: its sprung rhythm crams stress against stress until "dapple-dawn-drawn Falcon" and the "rolling level underneath him steady air" have to be spoken aloud, the mouth made to ride and rebuff the very wind the falcon rides. Hopkins was a Jesuit who had burned his early verse and vowed his whole gift to God, and the bird's sheer mastery breaks something open in him. At the turn, one word does the work of a theology: "Buckle" means both to clasp into glory and to crumple, and he refuses to choose. The proof comes in the last lines, a hearth's blue-bleak embers that fall, gall themselves, and gash gold-vermilion, beauty that lets out its fire only by breaking.

title: Song of Myself
author: Walt Whitman
extract: Do I contradict myself? Very well then I contradict myself, (I am large, I contain multitudes.)
blurb: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself": the line should land as arrogance and somehow arrives as an embrace. Song of Myself, the poem that opens Leaves of Grass, turns that first gesture into a promise to the reader, for whatever the speaker assumes, you shall assume, and the wall between two strangers goes thin as paper. Across fifty-two sections of free verse, Whitman pulls the whole republic into one long breathing line, the carpenter and the prostitute, the runaway slave and the president, no one set above another, because verse without meter refuses to rank a person. A child asks him what the grass is and he answers a dozen ways, each truer than the last, the common green of every dooryard pressed living into your hand. To read it is to feel a single self widen until it has room for everyone inside it, the boast at the poem's close arriving as nothing but the truth: you are large, you contain multitudes.

title: Suttree
author: Cormac McCarthy
extract: Dear friend now in the dusty clockless hours of the town when the streets lie black and steaming in the wake of the watertrucks
blurb: Dear friend now in the dusty clockless hours of the town when the streets lie black and steaming in the wake of the watertrucks. So the book opens, and that biblical swell never lets go: McCarthy spent nearly twenty years on these sentences, and he spends them all on the people Knoxville threw away. Cornelius Suttree has walked out on a family of standing to fish the Tennessee River from a houseboat moored at the edge of McAnally Flats, among the drunks and ragmen and whores the city files under nuisance. His friend Gene Harrogate, a grinning country boy, tunnels beneath the streets toward a bank vault and very nearly blows himself to pieces. There is a woman, Joyce, loved and lost. There is no plot to speak of, only a man drifting through the wreckage of the early 1950s while the Flats wait under a demolition order. And the miracle is the prose, which renders river silt and sewage in the music of Genesis, and hands these ruined lives the only monument they will ever get.

title: Jude the Obscure
author: Thomas Hardy
extract: Done because we are too menny.
blurb: At dusk a stonemason's boy lies in a field and watches the far lights of Christminster come on, the city of scholars and spires he is certain will one day take him in. It never will. Thomas Hardy's last novel is the story of Jude Fawley, who teaches himself Greek and Latin by candle while the university a few miles off keeps its gates shut to the poor, and of Sue Bridehead, the cousin he loves, as quick and contradictory and modern a woman as the century produced. Their refusal to marry on the world's terms, their flight, the slow closing of every door, build toward a scene so terrible Victorian readers begged Hardy to stop. A child leaves a note: Done because we are too menny. Few books have looked so steadily at how cruelly a society can punish wanting more than it was willing to allot you. Hardy never wrote fiction again.

title: Howl
author: Allen Ginsberg
extract: I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness, starving hysterical naked
blurb: It opens on a wail that never pauses to apologize: I saw the best minds of my generation destroyed by madness, starving hysterical naked. Allen Ginsberg wrote in one long breath line, clause after clause launched from the same word, who, until the poem becomes a tidal roll-call of the dispossessed and the visionary, the junkies and saints and burning scholars America had thrown away. Then the howl turns to name its devourer: Moloch, the iron god of money and machinery, eating his own children alive. By the final movement the rage gentles into something unbearably tender, a vow shouted across the wall of a madhouse to a friend locked away inside it. You do not so much read this poem as get pulled under by it. It turned grief into incantation and obscenity into a court case, and it still sounds like a match struck against the polite silence of a whole country.

title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
day: International Day of Innocent Children Victims of Aggression
extract: But they seem to know where they are going, the ones who walk away from Omelas.
blurb: Picture a city in summer, bells ringing, swallows over the rooftops, horses garlanded for the festival race, a place so happy you suspect at once that it must be a lie. It isn't. Le Guin then shows you the one cost: in a broom closet beneath the city sits a child, naked, fed on a half-bowl of cornmeal, never spoken to, and everyone in Omelas knows it is there. The whole radiant happiness of the place rests on that single, unredeemed misery, and they have agreed to it. This is the most quietly devastating thought experiment in American fiction, a story that hands you the oldest bargain in ethics and watches your face. Most stay, having reasoned themselves to peace. A few rise from the table and walk out the gate, on into a darkness even the author cannot describe. You will know, before the last line, exactly which one you are.

title: Nature
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
extract: I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all; the currents of the Universal Being circulate through me.
blurb: Cross a bare common at twilight, the snow still standing in the puddles, nothing lucky in your day, and feel a gladness rise that borders on fear: this is where Emerson begins. Then comes the sentence that started a literature. Standing on open ground, his head bathed in the blithe air, he feels the small self dissolve until he is nothing and sees everything, a transparent eyeball through which the currents of the universe pour. Nature is the founding document of American thought, the essay that told a young country it need not borrow its religion or its poetry from the Old World, because the woods past the door were scripture enough. Emerson wonders what we would do if the stars came out one night in a thousand years, how we would believe and adore, then reminds us they come out every night and we have stopped looking up. Read it and you start looking again.

title: Eugene Onegin
author: Alexander Pushkin
extract: My uncle's goodness is extreme, If seriously he hath disease; He hath acquired the world's esteem And nothing more important sees.
blurb: At her window past midnight, a country girl pours her whole heart onto the page to a man she has met once, certain she will love him forever. Tatyana's letter is the most famous declaration in Russian literature, and the cruelty of Eugene Onegin is what comes after: the bored dandy reads it, and turns her down with chilly kindness. Pushkin wrote the whole novel in sonnet-like stanzas of his own invention, so the verse keeps dancing, witty and offhand, even as it walks toward a senseless duel between two friends. Tatyana grows up; Onegin learns, too late, exactly what he refused. The genius is the symmetry: two letters across the years, the same two people, everything between them reversed. Few books have made regret this elegant, or shown so plainly how a life can be ruined by the pose of having seen through everything.

title: My Name Is Red
author: Orhan Pamuk
extract: I am nothing but a corpse now, a body at the bottom of a well.
blurb: A corpse calls up from the bottom of a well, and so begins one of the strangest, most ravishing murder mysteries ever written, narrated in turn by the dead man, a gold coin, a dog, a tree, the colour red itself, and Death. In the snowbound Istanbul of 1591, the Sultan's miniaturists are secretly illuminating a book in the forbidden Frankish manner, with its scandal of perspective and portraiture, its vanity of an individual hand, and one of them has killed to bury the blasphemy. Beneath the whodunit runs the real wound: a war between two ways of seeing the world, the Persian master who paints a horse as God remembers it and goes blind in holy perfection, against the Venetian who paints what one mortal eye happens to see. Threaded through is the patient, aching courtship of Black and the widow Shekure. Pamuk makes you feel that to choose a style is to lose your soul, and to fall in love is to risk it anyway.

title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
extract: We are such stuff As dreams are made on; and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
blurb: The sea heaves, a ship splits on the rocks, and a man on the shore has conjured the whole tempest from nothing, then watches his enemies wash up alive on his island. Prospero, exiled Duke turned sorcerer, has waited twelve years for this hour: the spirit Ariel at his command, the brother who betrayed him within reach, his daughter Miranda about to meet her first young man. And then, at the height of his power, he gives it all up. He breaks his staff, drowns his book, and forgives. The isle, Caliban tells us, is full of noises, sounds and sweet airs that give delight and hurt not, and the whole play shimmers with that strange music. Hear Prospero say we are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep, and you are hearing Shakespeare himself lay down his art. No farewell in the language is gentler, or more complete.

title: Bleak House
author: Charles Dickens
extract: London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather.
blurb: Fog everywhere: fog up the river, fog down the river, and at its densest heart the High Court of Chancery, where the suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce has dragged on so long that no living soul can say what it was first about. This is Dickens at his angriest and his grandest, the book where the antagonist is not a person but a process: a court that swallows fortunes and lifetimes at its own glacial pace, patient, impartial, and bottomless. Around that pit he assembles a whole nation. A great lady at Chesney Wold keeps a secret that could ruin her; a boy named Jo who sweeps a crossing and, knowing nothing and taught nothing, carries disease between the classes that swear they never touch. Two voices share the telling, one rising above the machine to watch it whole, the other Esther Summerson, who can measure the worth of everyone in England except herself. You come to it for the fog, and you leave unable to get it back out of your lungs.

title: Herzog
author: Saul Bellow
extract: If I am out of my mind, it's all right with me, thought Moses Herzog.
blurb: He writes letters he will never send. To the dead, to the living, to Nietzsche, to Eisenhower, to his analyst, to God, scrawled on scraps and composed in his head, a brilliant man cracking apart and unable to stop explaining himself. Moses Herzog has lost his wife to his best friend, lost the thread of his life, and the only thing his great learning can do is narrate his own collapse with unbearable wit. Few novels have so exactly caught the particular agony of the over-educated heart, the way intelligence becomes a torment when feeling overwhelms it, the way a mind talks and talks because it cannot bear what has happened to the marriage beneath it. And yet the book is funny, gorgeously, helplessly funny, Bellow's sentences spilling and looping with a vitality no breakdown can kill. To read it is to feel a mind save itself by the sheer act of putting everything into words, and to recognize, with a jolt, how much of your own grief you have tried to think your way out of.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
extract: My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.
blurb: In a shuttered room where every clock stopped at twenty to nine, a jilted bride sits in her yellowing wedding dress beside a cake gone gray with cobwebs, and a blacksmith's boy is brought in to play for her amusement and to fall hopelessly in love with the girl she is raising to break men's hearts. That boy, Pip, comes into a secret fortune and goes to London to become a gentleman, certain he knows who his benefactor is. He is wrong, and the error costs him nearly everything that ever loved him. What Great Expectations does that no Victorian novel quite matches is to let a man narrate his own snobbery from the inside: the older Pip tells the whole story in retrospect, so every page of his rise carries the aftertaste of his shame at Joe, the gentle blacksmith who loved him without wanting a thing in return. The cruelty of the book is that the hindsight repairs nothing. Pip sees exactly how he failed the man who raised him, and the seeing only sharpens the grief.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
extract: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart.
blurb: An axe, an old pawnbroker, a theory that some men are permitted to kill. Raskolnikov, a starving ex-student in a St. Petersburg July so hot the city itself seems delirious, talks himself into the murder to prove he is one of the extraordinary few who stand above the moral law. Then he discovers what no theory accounted for: that the mind keeps its own ledger, and a conscience cannot be reasoned out of existence. What follows is less a chase than a slow tightening, Raskolnikov circling the truth, the detective Porfiry circling him, until the only relief left is to be caught. Dostoevsky writes fever from the inside, the swarming streets and the cold sweat and the half-mad logic that feels, line by line, exactly like your own worst three a.m. And then, impossibly, he offers a way back, through the love of a woman who has nothing and forgives everything.

title: Sailing to Byzantium
author: W.B. Yeats
extract: An aged man is but a paltry thing, a tattered coat upon a stick.
blurb: That is no country for old men, the poem begins, and it means the whole teeming world: the young in one another's arms, the salmon-falls, the mackerel-crowded seas, everything that is born only to die. An aging man, his body a tattered coat upon a stick, can no longer bear to live inside that sensual music, so he sails the seas to the holy city of Byzantium, begging its sages to consume his heart away and gather him into the artifice of eternity. What Yeats wants is staggering and a little terrifying: to be taken out of nature altogether, to die out of the dying animal of the flesh and be reborn as a thing of hammered gold, a mechanical bird singing on a golden bough to keep a drowsy emperor awake. It is the oldest dream an artist has, made unbearably exact: to trade the warm body that perishes for the cold made thing that lasts, and to wonder, even then, whether it was worth the cost.

title: Snow Country
author: Yasunari Kawabata
extract: The train came out of the long tunnel into the snow country.
blurb: The train comes out of the long tunnel into the snow country, and the earth lies white under the night sky. A dilettante from Tokyo, Shimamura, watches a girl's face float in the dark train window, a far-off light flaring for an instant inside her eye, and never quite recovers from the beauty of something he cannot keep. In a hot-spring town buried in snow he takes up with Komako, a geisha who loves him with a fierceness that has nowhere to go, who keeps a diary no one will read and studies for a life that will not come. Kawabata names such devotion wasted effort, and makes the waste unbearably lovely: a woman pouring everything into a man too cool to be warmed, in a place so white and silent it seems to be erasing them both. Few books have wrung so much tenderness from futility, or left a love this whole and this hopeless glittering in the snow.

title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
extract: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
blurb: Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself, and with that sentence the whole of London opens like a flung-back window: a June morning after the war, Big Ben booming the hours into the air, a single ordinary day stretched wide enough to hold an entire life. Clarissa is giving a party tonight. But the prose refuses to stay with her, slipping from mind to mind across the city, into the thoughts of an old lover, a passing stranger, and Septimus Warren Smith, a shell-shocked young veteran who hears the dead singing in Regent's Park and can no longer bear the weight of being alive. Woolf finds the deepest things in the smallest gestures, the way a whole life can turn on a kiss remembered for thirty years. When word of a death reaches the lit, crowded party, you understand what the shimmering day has been building toward, and why ordinary happiness can suddenly feel like grace.

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
extract: yes I said yes I will Yes.
blurb: Everything happens on one ordinary Thursday in Dublin: a man eats a kidney for breakfast, attends a funeral, drifts through pubs and a newspaper office and a maternity hospital, and walks home well after midnight. Joyce poured the whole of a human mind into the passing hours, every flicker of memory and appetite and grief caught as it happens, until the inside of a head becomes the largest place there is. The book changes voice with every chapter, ventriloquizing newspaper headlines, a religious catechism, the entire history of English prose itself, daring you to keep up and rewarding you when you do. And it ends inside Molly Bloom, half-asleep beside her husband, her thoughts running on without a single full stop toward the most famous yes in all of literature. Few books have loved one human life this completely. Give it the patience it asks for, and a single Dublin day opens into the whole of being alive.

title: Independent People
author: Halldór Laxness
extract: A man is not independent unless he has the courage to stand alone.
blurb: On a patch of debt-soured marshland that better men called cursed, a sheep farmer raises a turf hut and renames the place Summerhouses, and for this freehold he has waited eighteen years as another man's hired hand. Bjartur owes nothing to anyone, and he will go on owing nothing though it costs him every person who loves him. His religion is independence, fierce as scripture and just as merciless, and Laxness lets you feel both its grandeur and the slow horror of what it tramples. The wonder of the book is Ásta Sóllilja, his stepdaughter, the flower of his life, the one soft thing in a world of frost and lungworm and unpaid debt, and the way his pride cannot keep itself from breaking her. Set on an island of sagas and snow, it holds an entire people's stubbornness in one stooped, unbending man, and it will leave you arguing with him long after the last page.

title: Emma
author: Jane Austen
extract: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.
blurb: You will think yourself smarter than Emma Woodhouse, and that is the trap. Handsome, clever, and rich, she sets about arranging the loves of everyone in Highbury, certain she can read a heart at a glance, and Jane Austen keeps you sealed so snugly inside Emma's head that you misread the village just as she does, charmed the whole way down. Then comes the picnic at Box Hill, where Emma, bored and dazzling, makes a small cruel joke at the expense of harmless, chattering Miss Bates, who is too poor and too kind to defend herself. Mr. Knightley's reproof afterward is so quiet and so exact that the laughter dies in your own throat. That is the wager of the novel: most books let you see more than the heroine, and Emma bets you will see exactly as little. The rebuke that humbles her humbles you, and you close the book knowing yourself a shade better than when you opened it.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
extract: 124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom.
blurb: A house on the edge of Cincinnati shakes with the rage of a dead infant. "124 was spiteful," the novel begins, and the venom belongs to a baby whose mother once cut her throat rather than let a slavecatcher carry her back into bondage. When the ghost returns in the flesh, a glutted, devouring young woman who calls herself Beloved, Sethe gives herself over to the daughter she killed, starving to feed a love that has no bottom. Toni Morrison wrote the unspeakable arithmetic of slavery from the inside: what it costs a mother to decide her child is better dead than owned, and what a life built on that choice does to the one who made it. The prose moves like grief itself, circling the thing it cannot say until it must. Few novels have looked so steadily at the worst love is capable of, or insisted so fiercely that the people who survived deserve to be remembered by name.

title: Nausea
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
extract: I exist. It is soft, so soft, so slow. And light: it seems as though it suspends in the air.
blurb: He stoops to pick up a pebble at the edge of the sea, means to skip it across the water, and finds he cannot: the thing in his hand has turned obscene, too solid, too there. So opens the diary of Antoine Roquentin, a historian washed up in a grey French port, watching the ordinary furniture of the world shed its names one by one, until a chestnut root in the public garden rears up before him as pure, naked existence, soft and black and monstrous, meaning absolutely nothing. This is the queasy vertigo Sartre named nausea: the discovery that nothing had to be, that you yourself are superfluous, that the tidy story by which a life seems to add up is paint brushed over a void. It should be unbearable, and very nearly is. Yet the book keeps one small light burning, a worn record turning in a café, a melody so clean it seems to exist as nothing around it does. You will not look at a chestnut tree, or your own hand, the same way again.

title: Tess of the d'Urbervilles
author: Thomas Hardy
extract: 'Justice' was done, and the President of the Immortals, in AEschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess.
blurb: Hardy called her a pure woman, and Victorian England never forgave him the phrase. Tess Durbeyfield, a country girl sent to claim kinship with a rich family who bear her ancestors' noble name, is ruined by a man who takes what she will not give. She buries the child, returns to work as a dairymaid in the green Vale of Talbothays, and there meets Angel Clare, who loves her purely until the night she tells him what was done to her. Then he leaves. The whole book aches with the injustice of it: that a world will worship a woman's beauty and damn her for surviving the worst it does to her. Hardy writes the Wessex fields and seasons with such tenderness that the cruelty cuts deeper against them. Read it for Tess herself, who keeps her goodness when goodness has cost her everything, and for the slow gathering dread of where such a world must finally drive her.

title: Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
extract: To the worm that first gnawed the cold flesh of my corpse, I dedicate as a fond remembrance these Posthumous Memoirs.
blurb: The author is dead, and that is the joke and the liberty of it. Brás Cubas dedicates his memoir to the first worm that gnawed his corpse, then tells the story of his life with the careless candour only a man past all consequence can afford. He pursues a married woman, drifts through an inheritance he did nothing to deserve, dreams up a miracle cure that will finally make his name, and confesses every petty vanity because the grave has made honesty cost him nothing. The chapters are tiny, some a single line, one made of nothing but punctuation, and the narrator keeps breaking off to needle you, the reader he can no longer be bothered to impress. Under all the wit, what aches is the sum it reaches: a charmed, squandered life, seen whole at last by the only man who can no longer fix it. Machado de Assis wrote the funniest book ever made from a wasted life, and somehow the saddest.

title: Requiem
author: Anna Akhmatova
extract: Can you describe this? And I said: I can.
blurb: Outside a Leningrad prison, a woman has stood in the same line for seventeen months, holding a parcel for a son who may already be dead, when the woman beside her, lips blue with cold, whispers, "Can you describe this?" and Akhmatova answers, "I can." Out of that promise comes Requiem, the cycle she could not write down because possessing it on paper would have meant her own arrest, and so she gave it line by line to a few trusted friends to carry in memory while the paper burned. It is the great poem of the Stalinist terror, told not from the cells but from the women left at the gate, and it will not keep the grief to itself: this is not one mother's anguish but a whole country's, queuing in the snow. Read it and you stand in that line too, learning what it costs to remember out loud when remembering is forbidden.

title: Bezhin Meadow
author: Ivan Turgenev
extract: It was a glorious July day, one of those days which only come after many days of fine weather.
blurb: Night comes down over the open steppe, and a hunter who has lost his way stumbles to the edge of a wide hollow where two fires burn and a circle of peasant boys sit guarding the horses till morning. He lies in the grass, pretends to sleep, and listens. The boys trade the stories children tell in the dark: the water-sprite laughing in the reeds, the drowned who will not lie still, the dead master hunting the meadow for his grass, the forest spirit that walks a man in circles until dawn. Around them Turgenev pours the whole Russian night, the warm dark and the smell of the grass, the firelight trembling on each frightened face, and he loves these boys with a tenderness that never once tips into pity. Then, in a single line at the close, he tells you which of them did not live out the year, and the whole long beautiful night turns into an elegy you did not know you were reading.

title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
extract: All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.
blurb: On a barn wall, a single law is painted that the animals can read by heart, and over the seasons a word is quietly added in the night, then another, until the law means its own opposite. Orwell called this small book a fairy story, and it has the clean cruelty of one. The beasts of Manor Farm rise up, drive out their drunken master, and swear that no creature shall ever again live under the boot, only to watch the pigs who led them swell into the very thing they overthrew. The heartbreak is Boxer, the great cart-horse whose answer to every hardship is that he will work harder, and who is sold to the knacker for a case of whisky the day his strength gives out. By the last page the others crowd to the farmhouse window, looking from pig to man and man to pig, and finding they can no longer tell which is which.

title: Notebook of a Return to the Native Land
author: Aimé Césaire
extract: my negritude is neither tower nor cathedral, it takes root in the red flesh of the soil
blurb: At the end of the small hours: the line tolls through the poem again and again, like surf returning to a shore, carrying Aimé Césaire home to Martinique to see it whole at last. He sees the hungry town and the rotting shacks, and on the streetcar the comic, degraded man he is ashamed to find himself laughing at with everyone else. And out of that shame, the poem turns volcanic. This is the work that gave the world the word négritude, and it does not argue for Black dignity so much as erupt with it, refusing the cold inheritance of conquest and claiming instead those who invented nothing, explored nothing, and gave themselves utterly to the living heart of the world. Watch the verse climb off its knees and stand, page by page, until the island itself seems to lift toward the sun. Read it aloud. It was built to land like a thunderclap, and it still does.

title: The Apology
author: Plato
extract: The unexamined life is not worth living.
blurb: Invited to name his own punishment after the verdict, Socrates proposes that the city should reward him instead, with free meals at public expense, the honor reserved for Olympic champions. This is a man on trial for his life, and he refuses to pretend he fears losing it. Plato's The Apology records the defense Socrates gave before five hundred Athenian jurors on charges of impiety and corrupting the young; "apologia" means defense, not contrition, and he apologizes for nothing. He calls himself a gadfly the god has fastened to the sluggish flank of Athens, stinging the great drowsy creature awake, and claims he is wise only in knowing how little he knows. Offered silence or exile, he answers that the unexamined life is not worth living, and takes the hemlock rather than become any other kind of man. Read it and you see why no argument since has had to prove itself at quite this price.

title: The Social Contract
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
extract: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains.
blurb: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." Rousseau opens with the sentence that would help topple a monarchy, then spends the rest of the book asking the question buried inside it: not how to break the chains, but how to make them just. His answer is the general will, the idea that a people can author the laws they live under and so obey only themselves, that authority drawn from the consent of the governed is the one authority that does not enslave. It is a thrilling, dangerous, impossibly hopeful proposition, that a crowd of strangers might become a single body politic and govern itself without a master. Read it knowing the Bastille fell within Rousseau's century and the men who stormed it carried his sentences in their heads. Few books have argued, this fiercely, that freedom and obedience could be the same act.

title: L'infinito
author: Giacomo Leopardi
extract: So my mind sinks in this immensity: and foundering is sweet in such a sea.
blurb: A young poet climbs a lonely hill outside a small provincial town, and a hedge blocks his view of the horizon. That is all that happens. From that one obstruction Leopardi builds the most astonishing fifteen lines in Italian, because the hedge hides the world and the mind is suddenly free to imagine what lies past it: interminable spaces, superhuman silences, a depthless calm so vast the heart nearly recoils in fear. Then the wind stirs the branches, and the sound of this living moment rings against that imagined eternity, until the seasons, dead and present, come flooding in. L'infinito is not about a view. It is about the strange sweetness of being overwhelmed, the mind consenting to drown in something larger than itself. The poem carries you to the edge of thought and lets you go, and its final line has lived in the memory of Italian readers for two centuries: to founder, it says, is sweet in such a sea.

title: A Song on the End of the World
author: Czesław Miłosz
extract: On the day the world ends a bee circles a clover, a fisherman mends a glimmering net.
blurb: A bee circles a clover and a fisherman mends his glimmering net, the way they would on any ordinary morning. This is the day the world ends, and Miłosz refuses it every sign we were promised: no thunder, no archangel's trumpet, no lightning to split the sky. There are only women under bright umbrellas and a drunkard growing sleepy at the edge of a lawn, and no one believes it is happening now. He wrote it in occupied Warsaw in 1944, while the world he knew was in fact burning around him, and the poem holds a terrible, quiet certainty: the apocalypse asks for no theatre, because it will look exactly like this, like nothing at all. At the end an old man who could have been a prophet kneels in his garden binding up tomatoes, and what he says, without once looking up, is the calmest and most frightening sentence ever written about the end of everything.

title: Journey to the End of the Night
author: Louis-Ferdinand Céline
extract: Travel is useful, it exercises the imagination.
blurb: Ferdinand Bardamu signs up for the war on a whim, chasing a passing band down a Paris boulevard, and by nightfall he is loose in a France gone mad with slaughter, having learned the one thing he will carry everywhere after: that he is a coward, and that cowardice may be the only sane answer to a world bent on killing him. From the trenches he flees, to a fever-rotted African colony, to the clanging assembly lines of Ford's Detroit, to a tubercular Paris slum where he hangs out a doctor's shingle among people too poor to be saved. Céline wrote it in a French nobody had dared set on the page, the gutter slang and broken rhythms and trailing ellipses of real speech, and made every polished sentence before him sound embalmed. This is the great novel of looking straight at the worst of us and refusing to flinch, of seeing that we are all traveling the same road into the same dark. Few books are this funny about despair, or this tender toward the ruined.

title: Siddhartha
author: Hermann Hesse
extract: I can think. I can wait. I can fast.
blurb: A seeker meets the Buddha himself, the fully awakened one, listens to a teaching that has no flaw in it, and then walks away. He cannot be given wisdom, Siddhartha understands; he must live it, every error of it, in his own body. So he plunges into the world he renounced: the courtesan Kamala teaching him love, the merchant teaching him greed, the dice and the wine teaching him despair, until a son he adores breaks his heart exactly as he once broke his father's. Then he comes to the river, and learns to listen to it. Hesse wrote this slim, luminous book out of his own collapse, and it carries the strange calm of someone who has stopped fighting the current. Its great gift is the river's secret, that time is not real and every voice of the world is one voice saying Om. Few books make peace feel so hard-won, or so close.

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Franz Kafka
extract: One morning, when Gregor Samsa woke from troubled dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a horrible vermin.
blurb: He wakes on his back, hard as armour, his thin legs waving helplessly above him, and his first clear thought is not terror but the train he is about to miss for work. Franz Kafka gives literature its most monstrous premise and then flatly refuses to explain it; the real horror is never that Gregor Samsa has become an insect, but that his family adjusts. Watch the love curdle into housekeeping: the locked door, the rotting scraps shoved under it, the sister whose violin he loved learning to flinch. This is the most exact thing ever written about being wanted only for what you provide, and about what remains of a person once the providing stops. Few books are so quietly unbearable about the small room you are kept in, the apple festering in your back, the morning they decide everyone would be lighter if you were simply gone.

title: Civil Disobedience
author: Henry David Thoreau
extract: That government is best which governs least.
blurb: One night in a Concord jail, held for refusing a tax to a government that kept slaves and waged war on Mexico, Thoreau worked out the most dangerous idea an honest person can have: that obedience to an unjust law is itself a kind of wrong. He will not lend his weight, not even the few coins of it, to a machine he believes is grinding men down. The argument is plain and merciless. If the law makes you the agent of injustice, then break the law; the true place for a just man under a government that imprisons unjustly is also a prison. What gives the essay its strange, quiet force is how personal it makes the question. It does not ask what governments should do. It asks what you will do, alone, when the tax collector knocks. The cell held him one night; the sentences he wrote there reached Gandhi's salt road and a Birmingham jail, and they are still knocking.

title: The Sun Also Rises
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: Isn't it pretty to think so?
blurb: Count the drinks. The Pernod, the Fundador, the cold Spanish wine drunk from a leather bag in the sun, the bottles emptied to keep the talking going and the wanting down. Jake Barnes loves Lady Brett Ashley and cannot have her: a wound from the war has seen to that, and the whole novel turns on the ache of a desire that can never be answered. So they drift, this circle of expatriates, from the cafés of Paris to the bullring at Pamplona, where Hemingway writes the running of the bulls and the grace of a young matador with a clean, unhurried attention that feels like prayer. The sentences are short and plain and somehow hold everything the characters will not say. Few books have made so much sorrow out of so little. By the last line you will understand exactly how it feels to want a thing you know you cannot keep, and to say so lightly anyway.

title: As I Lay Dying
author: William Faulkner
extract: My mother is a fish.
blurb: My mother is a fish, the youngest boy decides, having no other shape to hold his loss in. Addie Bundren has died, and her family loads the pine coffin her eldest son built beneath her window onto a wagon, then hauls it across forty miles of flooded river and scorched road to bury her in Jefferson, buzzards wheeling above the July heat. Faulkner splinters the telling among fifteen voices, fifty-nine short chapters, each Bundren and bystander speaking in turn, so you assemble the grief and the family's separate, secret hungers yourself. Addie gets a single chapter too, spoken from the far side of death, and it overturns everything you believed about why these people are on the road. The wonder is how he makes a mind audible: the broken syntax of a frightened child, a son's pride as he sets his own shattered leg, a father who longs for new teeth more than he mourns his wife. Grief has rarely been this funny, or this true.

title: The Pillow Book
author: Sei Shōnagon
extract: In spring it is the dawn that is most beautiful. In summer the nights.
blurb: "In spring, the dawn." So her book begins, and so it goes on, a thousand small acts of attention: the mountain rim slowly paling and flushed with red, fireflies adrift in the summer dark, wild geese shrunk to specks in a far autumn sky, snow fallen on a winter morning. Sei Shōnagon served the young empress Teishi in the Heian court, and into a private sheaf of paper she poured everything she noticed: things that make the heart beat faster, things that should be small, hateful things, the exact pleasures and irritations of a refined life. What undoes you is the nearness of her. A thousand years dissolve, and here is a living woman, dazzlingly sharp, helplessly alive to beauty, telling you precisely what delights and annoys her. To read it is to be handed a whole sensibility intact, proof that the texture of a single day, noticed hard enough, outlasts the court that made it.

title: Confessions of a Mask
author: Yukio Mishima
extract: What I wanted was to die among strangers, untroubled, beneath a cloudless sky.
blurb: In a reproduction of Guido Reni's Saint Sebastian, the martyr hangs lashed to a tree, arrows buried in his side, his head fallen back in an expression no one has taught the narrator to read as suffering. His body answers before his mind can object, and in that instant a schoolboy in wartime Japan learns the shape of a desire his country has no language to permit. What follows is a life built as performance. He worships a coarse, magnificent schoolmate named Omi from a distance he never closes, then courts a young woman, Sonoko, with a sincerity that is itself the most elaborate disguise, feeling the courtship and feeling nothing it is meant to mean. Mishima writes it all in prose cold and exact as surgery, a young man cataloguing his own concealment without once flinching. Do not wait for the mask to drop. His unbearable finding is that the confession is not the mask's undoing. It is the mask made flawless.

title: The Road Not Taken
author: Robert Frost
extract: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I-- I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.
blurb: Two roads diverge in a yellow wood, and a traveler stands a long while where they part, sorry he cannot walk both. Everyone knows how it ends: he takes the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference. But read the lines again. He admits the two paths are worn "really about the same," that the leaves that morning lay equal on each, and that the heroic sigh he imagines giving "ages and ages hence" is a story he is already rehearsing, before he has gone anywhere. The Road Not Taken is the most misread poem in English, and that is its quiet genius: it catches a mind in the act of inventing the meaning of its own life. Frost wrote it to tease a friend who agonized over every turning they had not taken. The trap is that you will finish it feeling vindicated, and never notice you were the one being teased.

title: Housekeeping
author: Marilynne Robinson
extract: My name is Ruth. I grew up with my younger sister, Lucille, under the care of my grandmother, Mrs. Sylvia Foster.
blurb: A glacial lake sits at the heart of Fingerbone, and it has already taken two of this family: the grandfather, when his train slid off the bridge one night and vanished without a ripple by morning, and years later the mother, who borrowed a car and drove it calmly into the same black water. Ruth and her sister Lucille are passed between relatives until their aunt Sylvie arrives to keep house, though Sylvie keeps it the way water keeps a shape. She sleeps in her coat, eats in the dark, lets the leaves drift in through doors left open, and saves the rinsed tin cans she will never use. Marilynne Robinson's first novel understands that ordinary housekeeping is a quiet refusal to grieve, a daily insistence that absence is manageable, and that Sylvie's failure at it is a deeper fidelity to the dead. The prose runs long and luminous, all cold light and rising water, until you feel the pull of the lake yourself, and the terrible tenderness of a girl who would rather drift than forget.

title: The Book of Laughter and Forgetting
author: Milan Kundera
extract: The struggle of man against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting.
blurb: In a café in a town she will never call home, Tamina pours coffee and strains to remember the colour of her dead husband's eyes. Her diaries, the whole record of their marriage, sit in a drawer in Prague she can no longer reach, and the harder she reaches the faster he dissolves. Around her loss Milan Kundera builds seven variations on a single unbearable idea: that forgetting is not a flaw of the mind but a force, sometimes a mercy and sometimes a weapon, and that a regime able to make a people forget owns them more completely than one that merely frightens them. He shows you a man airbrushed from a photograph until only his fur hat remains on a comrade's head, and the laughter of the faithful closing over the empty space. The struggle of man against power, he writes, is the struggle of memory against forgetting, and by the last page you believe him, and you are afraid for everything you have already begun to lose.

title: Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair
author: Pablo Neruda
extract: Tonight I can write the saddest lines.
blurb: Tonight I can write the saddest lines, a boy of nineteen tells himself, and a century of readers have whispered the same words back into their own dark rooms. Here Pablo Neruda makes a woman out of landscape, a body of white hills and white thighs that looks, he writes, like a world lying in surrender, and turns the oldest ache there is into something that feels like it happened to you last week. The poems move from the heat of having someone to the cold of the bed where she used to lie, and the closing Song of Despair goes down like a ship sinking with all its cargo of memory. He never pretends the grief is noble. He just says it, plainly: I no longer love her, that's certain, but maybe I love her. To read this is to be nineteen and wrecked by someone all over again.

title: Death and the King's Horseman
author: Wole Soyinka
extract: You did not save my life District Officer. You destroyed it.
blurb: At dusk in a Yoruba marketplace, the drums are summoning a man to his own death, and he goes toward it dancing in his finest cloth, flirting with the market women as he passes. The king is dead, and custom and cosmos require that Elesin Oba, his Horseman, follow him across the threshold by nightfall, willing himself to die so the world does not tear loose from its order. A colonial officer, certain he is saving a life, has him chained instead. Soyinka warned against shrinking this to a clash of cultures: the true reckoning is with the threshold, the crossing between the living, the dead, and the not-yet-born. Hear the language, dense with proverb and praise-song, a drumbeat beneath every line. And when the duty Elesin cannot finish falls to one who loves him too well to let it go undone, the play closes on a silence where his dance should have ended, a whole world left hanging in the balance.

title: Candide
author: Voltaire
extract: We must cultivate our garden.
blurb: The best of all possible worlds, Dr. Pangloss keeps insisting, even as that world hangs him, shakes Lisbon to rubble, and flogs his hapless pupil across two hemispheres. Voltaire wrote this little book in something close to fury and dressed it as a romp: earthquake, auto-da-fé, war, slavery, plague, each fresh catastrophe narrated at a sprint and with a perfectly straight face, until the comfortable doctrine that all suffering is secretly for the good lies in pieces on the floor. The marvel is how funny it stays while doing this, how lightly it carries its anger. Candide loses everything he was promised and keeps walking anyway. Then, after every grand system has failed him, arrives the quietest and most famous sentence in the book: we must cultivate our garden. Stop trying to justify the world; tend your own small corner of it. Read it in a single sitting, the way it was built to be swallowed whole.

title: The Sea The Sea
author: Iris Murdoch
extract: Time, like the sea, unties all knots.
blurb: Charles Arrowby has quit the London theatre to become, he announces, good: to repent of a lifetime's vanity in a cold house by the sea, eating his strange solitary feasts and writing it all down. Then, in the village below, he glimpses Hartley, the girl he loved at sixteen and lost, now an old woman married to a frightened man, and the whole project of his redemption curdles into obsession. He resolves to rescue her, to roll back the decades, to take back the one thing time stole. What Murdoch knows, and lets us watch with a dread that gathers like weather, is that a man narrating his own goodness is the last person alive who can see himself; every page of self-justification is a page of self-betrayal. The sea broods through all of it, beautiful and indifferent, and throws up a monster no one else can see. Few novels have so generously, so cruelly, caught the human gift for mistaking possession for love.

title: The Prelude
author: William Wordsworth
extract: Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, But to be young was very Heaven!
blurb: A boy skates alone across a frozen lake at dusk, leans back on his heels to stop, and the cliffs keep wheeling past him as though the earth itself were still turning under his feet. William Wordsworth called episodes like this his "spots of time," moments of fear and wonder from a Lake District boyhood that lodged so deep they went on feeding the imagination for the rest of his life. The Prelude is the long blank-verse account of how those moments made a poet, the first epic whose whole subject is the growth of a single ordinary mind, formed not by war or gods but by ice and starlight and the slow work of mountains. Its argument, earned line by line, is that nature does not merely please the mind, it shapes it, through terror as much as beauty. Wordsworth wrote at it for fifty years and never let it print while he lived, a poem to Coleridge, his dearest friend, about a self he could not finish becoming.

title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
day: World Day for International Criminal Justice
extract: Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning, without his having done anything wrong, he was arrested.
blurb: Someone must have been telling lies about Josef K. He wakes on an ordinary morning to find two men in his room, eating his breakfast, informing him he is under arrest. They will not say for what. No charge ever comes, and no court will name itself; there is only an endless, courteous machinery that seems to know something about his guilt he himself does not. He hires lawyers, petitions clerks, climbs to stifling attic tribunals, and the case only deepens by never being stated. Kafka caught a dread no one had named before him: the suspicion that you are guilty of something everyone agrees on but no one will name, an accusation that never arrives to be answered. Read the parable of the man who waits his whole life at the door of the Law, the gatekeeper, the light he glimpses too late. It is the most accurate nightmare ever written, and it does not let you wake.

title: Vanity Fair
author: William Makepeace Thackeray
extract: Which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied?
blurb: The carriage pulls away from the academy and Becky Sharp, penniless and twenty and finished with being grateful, hurls the schoolmistress's parting gift, a dictionary, back into the dust. So begins the most thrilling climb in English fiction: a governess with no fortune and an absolute genius for charm, working her way into drawing rooms that would never have her, fooling everyone, owing everyone, afraid of no one. Thackeray called it a novel without a hero, and he meant it as a confession. His real subject is the whole vain market of ambition, where Waterloo is fought offstage while London frets about its gowns, where nearly everyone is for sale and most are glad of it. Becky is monstrous and you will adore her, which is precisely the trap, and the book never lets you feel clean about it. Its last words leave the carnival hanging on a question: which of us has his desire, or, having it, is satisfied?

title: The Emperor of Ice-Cream
author: Wallace Stevens
extract: Let be be finale of seem.
blurb: Call the roller of big cigars. The poem opens like an order shouted into a busy kitchen, and at once the room is loud with the living: a muscular man whipping concupiscent curds in cracked cups, boys hauling flowers in last month's newspaper, girls loitering in their everyday dresses. Wallace Stevens loved a word the way a child loves sugar, and he lets these consonants clatter and melt on the tongue. Then, in the cold back bedroom, a dead woman lies under a sheet she once embroidered with fantails, her horny feet protruding, in the poem's own unsparing phrase, to show how cold she is, and dumb. Set the riot of appetite against the silent corpse and ask which one rules. Stevens answers without blinking: against death there is no king and no god, only the body's hunger for sweetness while it can still taste. The only emperor is the emperor of ice-cream.

title: Blood Meridian
author: Cormac McCarthy
extract: War is the ultimate game because war is at last a forcing of the unity of existence. War is god.
blurb: Riders cross a desert lit like the floor of hell, the sun coming up red over the mountains, and McCarthy's prose tolls after them in long Old Testament cadences that make you stop and read the line twice. These are the Glanton gang, scalp-hunters turned loose on the Texas-Mexico borderlands of the 1840s, and at their center rides Judge Holden: hairless, enormous, impossibly learned, the most frightening figure in American fiction, who holds that war is the eternal condition of man, that war is god. The novel refuses every consolation the western ever promised. No justice waits out in the dust, only the violence and the going on, set down in sentences so beautiful they feel like a kind of blasphemy. What stays with you is not the slaughter but the judge's argument, made in that vast and unhurried voice, that the world has always run on blood and that he is merely its high priest. Close the book and the desert is still there, the dance still turning, and you cannot quite say he was wrong.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
blurb: Far out where no other boat will follow, an old Cuban fisherman feels a great fish take his bait in the dark, and for two days and nights he holds the line across his shoulders while the marlin tows his skiff toward the open Gulf. Santiago has gone eighty-four days without a catch, and he comes to love the fish even as he kills it, calling it brother, grieving that the same pride binds them both. Hemingway pares every sentence to the bone, the prose so clean and unhurried it moves like the sea itself, and the old man's murmured talk to the bird, to the boy, to his own cramping hand carries a tenderness his hard life never let him say aloud. Then the sharks come for what he has earned, and you watch a triumph turn to wreckage while the man inside it stays unbroken. He brings home only a skeleton lashed to his skiff, and falls asleep dreaming of lions on the long beaches of his youth.

title: Arcadia
author: Tom Stoppard
extract: We shed as we pick up, like travellers who must carry everything in their arms.
blurb: Stir the jam into the rice pudding and you can never stir it back out: this, a thirteen-year-old reasons at the schoolroom table at Sidley Park, is why time runs one way and the whole warm universe is cooling toward silence. Thomasina Coverly has glimpsed the heat death of everything long before the physicists, between Latin lessons and questions about what a carnal embrace might be. Two hundred years later, in the very same room, modern scholars sift the same papers, chase Lord Byron, and get it gloriously wrong. Stoppard lets both centuries crowd one table until their props and people overlap, and the play turns on everything we know and lose and stumble back upon, the pull of bodies in heat that Newton left out of his equations. It ends in a waltz between the girl and her tutor, a borrowed candle, the eve of her seventeenth birthday, and a dread you feel gathering in the small flame she carries up to bed.

title: The Cairo Trilogy
author: Naguib Mahfouz
extract: Nothing records the effects of a sad life so graphically as the human body.
blurb: For years Amina is not allowed past her own front door; she knows Cairo only through the wooden lattice of an upstairs window, watching the minarets catch the dawn while her husband sleeps off a night she is forbidden to imagine. By day he is the most pious and terrifying of fathers; by night, al-Sayyid Ahmad is the most charming man in the cafés, full of wine and song. Naguib Mahfouz follows this one household down three generations and a quarter-century, from the 1919 streets where Egyptians rise against the British to the slow loosening of everything the father's word once held absolute. Sons drift toward faith, doubt, and politics; one of them does not come home. What Mahfouz builds, room by room and prayer by prayer, is time itself: the unbearable tenderness of watching a whole world that seemed permanent become the past while you read. By the end you have not read about a family. You have lived inside one and outlived it.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
extract: All human wisdom is summed up in these two words,--'Wait and hope.'
blurb: Edmond Dantès has everything a young man could want: a ship to captain, a girl to marry, a future bright as the Marseille harbour at dawn. Then, at his own betrothal feast, four men who envy him put their names to a lie, and he vanishes into the Château d'If, the island fortress from which no prisoner returns. What he finds there, whispered through stone by a dying priest, is a fortune beyond counting and the name of every man who buried him alive. The rest is the most patient revenge ever written: a stranger of impossible wealth arriving in Paris years on, gracious, smiling, holding every thread in his gloved hand. Dumas built it as pure thrill, and it thrills, but beneath runs a darker question, whether any ransom can buy back a stolen life, and where a wronged man stops being the hand of Providence and starts playing God. Wait and hope, the novel says at its close. By then you will know the cost of both.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
extract: But I don't want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness. I want sin.
blurb: In a sunlit nursery, infants crawl toward bowls of roses and bright picture books, and then the floor shrieks with electricity until they learn to recoil from flowers and reading for life. This is happiness, engineered. Huxley imagines a civilization that has solved the human problem by deleting it: babies decanted from bottles into fixed castes, every want met, every grief dissolved on the tongue by a gram of soma, mothers and fathers and solitude and old age all scrubbed away. It is a paradise, which is exactly the horror. When a man raised on Shakespeare outside the system wanders in, he asks for the one thing it cannot grant him: the right to be unhappy, to grow old, to love something he might lose. No book has guessed more chillingly that the cage might be soft, scented, and gladly chosen, that we would not be tortured out of our freedom but comforted out of it.

title: The Woman in the Dunes
author: Kōbō Abe
extract: Do you shovel to survive, or survive to shovel?
blurb: A man comes to the coast for a weekend, an amateur entomologist hunting a beetle that lives in the dunes, and accepts a night's lodging in a house at the bottom of a sand pit, reached by a rope ladder. In the morning the ladder is gone. Below him a woman shovels sand that never stops falling, sand that buries the walls by dawn, sifts into the rice, the lungs, the skin, the act of love. Abe writes the stuff with such hallucinatory exactness that you feel it grinding between your own teeth. The terror is how ordinary the trap becomes: dig or be buried, and the digging starts to feel like a reason to live. What makes the novel unbearable is the doubt it plants about the life he left behind in the city, the salaried days, the apartment he was so sure of, whether any of that was freedom either. By the end you cannot say which side of the ladder you are on.

title: A Hero of Our Time
author: Mikhail Lermontov
extract: I was prepared to love the whole world--no one understood me: I learned to hate.
blurb: On a ledge above a Caucasus ravine, Pechorin chooses the ground for a duel: whoever is hit must topple onto the rocks below. He is the most magnetic man in any room and the coldest, an officer who seduces, schemes, and breaks the people foolish enough to love him, then turns the same merciless eye on himself. The novel refuses to hand him over directly. We meet Pechorin first through an old soldier who adored him, glimpse him once on a mountain road, and only afterward are let into his journal, where the verdict is brutal: a brilliant man with nothing worth spending himself on, boredom curdled into cruelty. Lermontov called him a portrait assembled from the vices of an entire generation, and meant it as an accusation. Out of this restless, clear-eyed wreck the whole line of Tolstoy and Dostoevsky would come. Read it for the vertigo of recognizing yourself in a man you could never forgive.

title: A Farewell to Arms
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places.
blurb: In the late summer of that year the troops march past a house on a river, and the dust they raise powders the leaves of the trees so they fall early. That is how the book begins, in a prose so clean it seems to have had everything inessential burned off it, every word load-bearing, every short sentence a held breath. Frederic Henry, an American driving ambulances for the Italian army, finds Catherine Barkley in a war he no longer believes in, and what starts as a way to pass the nights becomes the only thing either of them has. Hemingway writes their happiness so plainly that you trust it completely, which is the trap, because the rain keeps falling and Catherine is afraid of the rain. Few novels know so exactly that the world breaks everyone, and that it kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. Read it for the tenderness that survives all the way to the last cold page.

title: Mahabharata
author: Vyasa
extract: What is found here may be found elsewhere. What is not found here will not be found elsewhere.
blurb: Two vast armies face each other across the plain of Kurukshetra, cousin against cousin, and the finest archer alive lets his bow slip from his hand: the men he has been brought here to kill are his uncles, his teachers, the boys he grew up beside. Into that paralysis his charioteer leans close and begins to speak, and the charioteer is God. The Bhagavad Gita is only one current in the largest river of story ever told, a poem that swallows a dice game in which a king gambles away his kingdom, his brothers, and his wife; a thirteen-year exile; a war that ends with the earth emptied of its young men. It says of itself that whatever is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not here exists nowhere, and after living inside it you believe the boast. It is the whole of human wanting, and the terrible bill that wanting comes to.

title: A Modest Proposal
author: Jonathan Swift
day: World Day Against Trafficking in Persons
extract: A young healthy child well nursed is, at a year old, a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food.
blurb: It begins in the calm, civic voice of a man who has done his arithmetic. He has counted the beggars in Dublin's streets, weighed the cost of their children against the nation's wealth, and arrived, regretfully, sensibly, at a solution: that the infants of the Irish poor be fattened and sold to the tables of the rich, a delicacy at a year old, the skin good for gloves. Jonathan Swift never once raises his voice. That is the horror, and the genius. The essay reasons so coolly, cites such tidy figures, anticipates objections so courteously, that you understand with a cold drop in the stomach exactly what indifference looks like when it learns to speak like policy. It is the most savage thing ever written about the way the comfortable discuss the starving, and it works because it refuses, to the last decorous sentence, to wink. Read it and you will never trust a reasonable tone again.

title: If This Is a Man
author: Primo Levi
extract: Consider if this is a man who works in the mud, who does not know peace, who fights for a scrap of bread.
blurb: Consider whether this is a man, the opening poem demands: one who labors in the mud and fights for a crust of bread. Primo Levi wrote it after eleven months in the Auschwitz subcamp at Monowitz, a chemist's exact eye turned on the machinery built to unmake the human being. He watches a guard snatch an icicle from his thirsting mouth and answer his "why" with "Hier ist kein warum," here there is no why, and you understand in one stroke a whole world emptied of reason. What astonishes is the calm: no rage, no vengeance, only the patient witness of a scientist cataloguing how a person is reduced to a number, a hunger, a thing that competes for soup. And then, against all that, a half-remembered canto of Dante recited to a friend, proof that some unkillable scrap of the man survives. Read it for the cold, miraculous mercy of being told the exact truth.

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
extract: Call me Ishmael.
blurb: A man with one leg, who lost the other to a white whale, stands on the deck of a Nantucket whaler and nails a gold coin to the mast: it belongs to the first sailor who sights the beast that maimed him. From this Herman Melville builds something far larger than a sea chase. The Pequod carries men of every race and faith toward a creature that has stopped being an animal and become the face of everything indifferent and enormous that a person can hate: God, the ocean, the blank white nothing behind the world. The prose swells like Shakespeare let loose on the Atlantic, lurching from a chapter on the colour white into sermons, soliloquies, the dense beautiful tedium of how to butcher a whale. You feel the wave gathering long before it breaks. Few books reach so high and pull the whole sky down with them.

title: Go Tell It on the Mountain
author: James Baldwin
extract: Everyone had always said that John would be a preacher when he grew up, just like his father.
blurb: On the morning of his fourteenth birthday, John Grimes works a dustrag across the front room of the Harlem apartment and watches the grime settle back the instant he lifts it, dirt ground so deep into the walls and the skin of his family that no labor will ever clear it. His stepfather Gabriel preaches with an authority that never bends toward love, and the long central movement breaks open the prayers of the saints around him, each carrying a Southern inheritance of whippings, shame, and flight that John is too young to read in their faces. That night he falls to the threshing floor of the Temple of the Fire Baptized, and Baldwin writes salvation with such bodily force you feel the boards beneath his back. Is it grace, or the only door out of a house Gabriel has made unlivable? The whole book breathes in King James cadence, the tongue Baldwin himself preached in as a teenager, and it is unbearable to watch a boy reach for deliverance in a language no one ever gave him freely.

title: Lord Jim
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: He was an inch, perhaps two, under six feet, powerfully built.
blurb: Eight hundred pilgrims sleep below deck on a steamer crossing the Indian Ocean when something underwater strikes the hull, and a rusted bulkhead begins to bulge against the sea. Jim is the young first mate who has rehearsed heroism his whole life in daydreams, and in the one moment it is asked of him for real, his body jumps into a lifeboat without him. The ship does not sink. He is left alive, stripped of his certificate, a coward by one leap he can never take back, and Conrad, who first went to sea at sixteen, knew the unbearable thing this book knows: that you are not the brave figure of your own imagining, only the person you were in the second your body chose for you. Marlow narrates in long, circling sentences that close on Jim from every angle and never quite hold him. He flees east to a river settlement that crowns him Lord and offers a second chance to prove what he is. You read on dreading, and half hoping, the moment it comes for him again.

title: Ozymandias
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
extract: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!
blurb: Somewhere in a desert, two enormous stone legs stand with nothing above them, and half-sunk in the sand nearby lies a shattered face still wearing a sneer of cold command. The pedestal keeps its inscription perfectly: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The command survives; the works do not. The kingdom is gone, the boundless and bare sands stretch away in every direction, and the one thing the centuries chose to spare is the boast that everything around it has turned to mockery. Shelley fits the whole death of empire into fourteen lines, and folds inside them a quieter marvel: the unnamed sculptor who read a tyrant's contempt so well that his hand outlived the man, the throne, and the civilization that built it. Every power that has called itself eternal has a desert like this one waiting. Here is the poem that knows the way there.

title: Boule de Suif
author: Guy de Maupassant
extract: And Boule de Suif still wept, and sometimes a sob she could not restrain was heard in the darkness between two verses of the song.
blurb: Snow on the road out of Rouen, a stalled stagecoach, ten respectable refugees who forgot to pack any food. Only the woman they sneer at, a plump prostitute the others call Butterball, has thought to bring a hamper, and within hours even the two nuns are gratefully accepting her chicken while the bourgeois who scorned her grow warm over her wine. Then a Prussian officer halts the coach at an inn and will not let it go on until she comes to his bed. She refuses, blazing with patriotic fury, and the same passengers who ate her food spend three days reasoning her into it, recasting surrender as sacrifice, as duty, as a kindness. Boule de Suif is the story Flaubert hailed as a masterpiece, and it shuts like a trap: confine these people, starve them a little, and watch how fast virtue rearranges itself around appetite. The cruelty that lasts is not the Prussian's. It is the silence of the good people on the carriage next morning, eating their own provisions, with nothing left to say to her.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
author: Kurt Vonnegut
extract: So it goes.
blurb: Beneath Dresden, in a cellar under the slaughterhouse numbered five, a young American prisoner waits out the night the sky catches fire and the city overhead burns to ash. Billy Pilgrim survives, and afterward comes unstuck in time, skidding without warning between his captivity, his daughter's wedding, his own death, and the planet Tralfamadore, whose aliens insist that all moments exist at once, so the dead are never gone, only elsewhere on the line. Each time death arrives, and it arrives on nearly every page, the book answers only "So it goes," three flat words that are not a shrug but the sound of a man who walked through the ashes and found no language equal to them. Kurt Vonnegut needed more than twenty years to write this, and what he made is less a war novel than a wound in the shape of one. Read it and you will never hear those three words the same way again.

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
extract: What is the meaning of life? That was all - a simple question; one that tended to close in on one with years.
blurb: Candles are lit, the boeuf en daube carried steaming to the table, and around it on a Scottish island Mrs. Ramsay watches her family and guests cohere, for one hour, into something that feels eternal. She is the gravity of the house, the warmth every restless longing bends toward, and looking at the candlelight she thinks that of such moments the thing is made that endures. Then Woolf does the most devastating thing in modern fiction: she empties the house. The years pour through the abandoned rooms, the war arrives, and Mrs. Ramsay's death is set down inside square brackets, a world ended in a subordinate clause while the wind keeps lifting the curtains in the dark. Years later Lily Briscoe comes back to the easel she abandoned before the war, the canvas unfinished, the woman who once filled it now gone to a shape of absence. To take up that brush at all is the book's whole faith: that against everything time carries off, one evening at a table, one line drawn true, might be made to hold.

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
author: Albert Camus
extract: One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
blurb: The boulder reaches the summit, balances a moment, and rolls back down the far slope. Sisyphus turns and walks after it, and it is in that walk down, Camus tells us, that the man is most alive, the hour of consciousness in which he sees his whole fate and is not crushed by it. The essay opens with a sentence that has frightened readers for generations, that the only truly serious philosophical question is suicide, and from there it refuses every comfort that would let us look away. Camus calls this collision the absurd: a mind that aches for meaning set against a universe that will not answer. To leap toward God, or reason, or hope, he names philosophical suicide, an escape from the confrontation rather than a passage through it. Written in occupied Paris, where despair held every card, the book chooses revolt, not the vanishing of the rock but the refusal to be beaten by it. One must imagine Sisyphus happy, it ends, and walking down the mountain beside him, you believe it.

title: Aubade
author: Philip Larkin
extract: I work all day, and get half-drunk at night. Waking at four to soundless dark, I stare.
blurb: Work all day, get half-drunk at night, then wake at four to soundless dark and stare. From that bare opening Philip Larkin builds the most clear-eyed poem in the language about the fear of dying, and he refuses every exit. Religion he calls a vast moth-eaten musical brocade made to pretend we never die; the philosopher's reassurance that no rational being can fear a thing it will not feel he answers flatly, because the not-feeling is exactly the horror, the sure extinction of sight and sound and touch and the mind that knows them. Aubade borrows the shape of a dawn love song, but the only thing approaching at first light is the same dread it began with, dressed as an ordinary morning of telephones and postmen. What makes it bearable, strangely, is its refusal to lie to you. To read it at four in the morning is to find, in the one poet who will not pretend, a kind of company.

title: Oblomov
author: Ivan Goncharov
extract: Mechanically and at random he traced some letters in the dust with his finger. There resulted the word Oblomovstchina.
blurb: The dressing gown is Persian, vast, worn soft from years of wear; the divan has long since taken the shape of its owner. For something close to a hundred and fifty pages, Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, a Russian gentleman of thirty-two with a steady income and an estate going quietly to ruin, tries to get out of bed and cannot. Visitors come and go, each busier and hollower than the last, while Goncharov watches his hero fail to rise with a tenderness that slowly becomes the argument: this stillness is worth our whole attention. Oblomov even gave a word to the language, Oblomovism, for the sweet paralysis of a man who would rather dream his life than live it. Yet the book loves him far too much to leave it a diagnosis. When Olga nearly wakes him, and he nearly lives, you lean toward the page; when he sinks at last into the warm, fed, undemanding calm of a widow's house, the grief is real, because he understood exactly what he was trading away, and chose the divan anyway.

title: Sonny's Blues
author: James Baldwin
extract: The tale of how we suffer, and how we are delighted, and how we may triumph is never new, it always must be heard.
blurb: He learns it from a newspaper on the subway home from teaching, his younger brother Sonny arrested for heroin, the name rising out of the print like something long dreaded. James Baldwin's Sonny's Blues holds two brothers apart and will not let either one go: the algebra teacher who took the respectable path, and the younger brother who chose the blues, and the trouble that came with it. For most of the story Sonny's choice looks like ruin, and his brother watches it the way you watch weather you cannot stop. Then, in a small downtown club, the bandleader Creole hands Sonny the piano, and the music begins to say what neither man could ever speak aloud, suffering taken apart in front of strangers and handed back as something survivable. This is Baldwin's deepest claim, that no one is truly heard until the listener stops protecting himself from what the other knows. The Scotch and milk the narrator sends up glows and shakes above the piano like the very cup of trembling.

title: Hills Like White Elephants
author: Ernest Hemingway
extract: The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white.
blurb: Heat off the dry hills, a bamboo bead curtain stirring across the doorway, two glasses sweating on a station table in the valley of the Ebro while a man and a girl wait for the express to Madrid. They order beer, then Anis del Toro, then beer again, and around every drink circles the one thing he wants and she does not: an abortion, a word Hemingway never lets either of them say. He calls it simple, just to let the air in, nothing really at all; she looks at the long white hills and says they look like white elephants, then quietly takes it back. In five pages you watch how gentle reasonableness becomes a kind of force, how a person can be talked toward something while both pretend the choice is hers. This is the iceberg made flesh, everything that matters held just below the surface, the silence saying what no speech could. The hills stay across the valley, long and white, and no one crosses them.

title: The Birth of Tragedy
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
extract: Only as an aesthetic phenomenon is existence and the world eternally justified.
blurb: When King Midas at last cornered the satyr Silenus and demanded to know what is best for man, the wise companion of Dionysus laughed and said: best never to have been born, and next best to die soon. This is the abyss Nietzsche believed the Greeks stared straight into, and his wonder is that they answered it not with despair but with tragedy, the most life-affirming art ever made. He finds two gods at its root. Apollo casts the beautiful, bounded dream-image over the horror; Dionysus, god of music and intoxication, dissolves the trembling self back into the whole; and their union on a stage lets a whole people look at suffering and still say yes.
