From this comes the vertiginous claim at its heart, that only as an aesthetic phenomenon are existence and the world eternally justified. A young classicist wrote it, his own discipline recoiled, and everything Nietzsche would become is already dancing here.

title: Nostromo
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: Any one can declaim about these things, but I pin my faith to material interests.
blurb: On the Golfo Plácido, a gulf so black a man cannot see his own hands, Nostromo rows a lighter heavy with silver into the dark to keep it from a revolution. He is the most trusted man in Sulaco, an Italian capataz whose entire fortune is what the docks believe of him: that he cannot be bought. Conrad invented a whole South American republic, Costaguana, its mountains and feuds and ruined idealists, only to set one silver mine at its heart and watch what the metal does to everyone who touches it. Charles Gould gives his soul to the lode until his wife Emilia loses the husband to the institution he becomes. And the silver, once buried, begins its slow work on the one incorruptible man, who can neither return it nor stop guarding it. Conrad tells it all out of order, the cost felt before the accounting, so you grasp too late what material interests truly take: not a man's honesty, but the self he most needed to believe in.

title: A Passage to India
author: E.M. Forster
extract: they said in their hundred voices, "No, not yet," and the sky said, "No, not there."
blurb: Boum. That is the only sound the Marabar Caves return, the same dead syllable for a hymn, a footstep, or a whispered name, and into that flattening echo Forster sends a hopeful little picnic that will not survive it. Dr. Aziz, a warm, quicksilver Indian doctor, has befriended two Englishwomen newly off the boat and still convinced that ordinary decency can reach across the Raj. In the dark of the caves something happens, or seems to, and an accusation rises that splits the colonial station along its racial seam. Forster never tells you what occurred underground, because the not-knowing is the whole subject: how empire makes meaning itself impossible between two people who might, under any other sky, have been friends. The kindest Englishman in the book stands by Aziz and still cannot hold the friendship together. At the close, two men ride out wanting to embrace, and the horses swerve apart; the earth says not yet, and the sky says not here.

title: To His Coy Mistress
author: Andrew Marvell
extract: Had we but world enough, and time, this coyness, Lady, were no crime.
blurb: Had we but world enough, and time, the poem begins, and for a few luxurious lines it lets us believe we do: a hundred years to praise her eyes, two hundred to adore each breast, thirty thousand for the rest. Then comes the most famous swerve in English love poetry, "But at my back I always hear / Time's wingèd chariot hurrying near," and the spell of leisure shatters. Marvell's seducer is too honest to flatter; he argues, and the argument is death itself. The grave is a fine and private place, he warns her, but none embrace there, and worms will try what her long caution has preserved. What makes the poem ache rather than merely dazzle is that the case for pleasure traps the one who makes it: the chariot is at his back too. By the close he is not pleading but blazing, urging that they tear their pleasures with rough strife through the iron gates of life. Read it once and every clock in the room grows louder.

title: Crow
author: Ted Hughes
extract: But who is stronger than death? / Me, evidently. / Pass, Crow.
blurb: Something is interrogating a newborn thing: who owns these scrawny little feet? Death. This bristly scorched-looking face? Death. These unspeakable guts? Death. And then, at the end of the catechism, who is stronger than death? Me, evidently. Pass, Crow. Ted Hughes wanted the songs a crow would actually sing, in a language stripped to something super-simple and super-ugly, and what came out was Genesis rewritten as black comedy by a creature to whom the worst has already happened. God tries to teach Crow the word Love, and Crow's gape produces a white shark, then a bluefly, a tsetse, a mosquito, then a man's head and a woman's body locked together in a struggle God cannot pull apart. It is horribly funny until it stops being funny. Hughes wrote these poems in the years after Sylvia Plath's death and abandoned the sequence when a second death made the rest unwriteable, so the myth breaks off mid-creation, exactly where its maker could not follow.

title: Critique of Pure Reason
author: Immanuel Kant
extract: Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind.
blurb: Look up from the room around you, and from the minutes sliding past as you read: Kant's claim is that neither the space nor the time is out there in the world. Both are the mind's own architecture, fitted to raw sensation before any experience can arrive, which is why mathematics holds without fail and why the world as it stands in itself, untouched by any mind, is sealed away for good. This is the largest question a book can shoulder, what a thinking creature can know and where that knowing must stop, and Kant, returning to it at fifty-seven after a decade of near-silence, gives it no quarter. The book is slow, asking to be read more than once before the whole system stands clear, but the vertigo waiting inside lives nowhere else: the ordinary world is partly your own mind's making. That, Critique of Pure Reason insists, is no loss to mourn but the one condition under which anything becomes knowable, the mind no mirror held up to reality but the light by which reality first appears.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
extract: No man, for any considerable period, can wear one face to himself, and another to the multitude, without finally getting bewildered.
blurb: The town means the letter as a brand. Hester Prynne, handed a scrap of cloth that marks her for life as an adulteress, takes up her needle and works it in gold thread, fantastic and gorgeous, until the badge of her shame becomes the most beautiful thing in drab Puritan Boston. That single act of defiance is the whole book in miniature. Hawthorne lets her wear the worst the magistrates can devise out in the open, year upon year, until it stops being a sentence and becomes simply hers, while the minister Arthur Dimmesdale, who shares the sin and hides it, is eaten from within by the secret he cannot speak. The wild child Pearl, born of that sin, is the one soul in town who cannot be taught to pretend. What The Scarlet Letter knows, and never stops knowing, is that a shame carried in the open can be outlived, and that the letter at last indicts not the woman who wears it but the people who pinned it on.

title: The Passion According to G.H.
author: Clarice Lispector
extract: I'm searching, I'm searching. I'm trying to understand.
blurb: Expecting a servant's clutter, a Rio sculptor steps into the maid's vacated room and finds instead a scoured desert: white walls, a bare cot, three charcoal figures drawn on the plaster like a cave painting. Then the wardrobe door, and inside it a cockroach, and the slow horror of crushing it so that a white paste wells from the wound. From this nothing, a clean room and a dying insect, Clarice Lispector builds one of the strangest spiritual ordeals in fiction. G.H., who has only initials, stops being a person across a single afternoon, peeled down past name and self until she reaches the oldest living matter, the neutral thing that simply is, indifferent to being loved or named. The novel ends in a reverse communion that you will not forget and may not forgive. Lispector writes in a continuous, groping present, language sent back into the place where language gives out, and somehow it holds.

title: King Lear
author: William Shakespeare
extract: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is To have a thankless child!
blurb: Tell me how much you love me, says an old king, and I will measure out my kingdom by the answer. Two daughters lie beautifully; the third, Cordelia, can only say she loves him as a daughter should, no more, no less, and for that honesty she is cast out. King Lear is the play in which Shakespeare withdraws every comfort he grants elsewhere: no innocence is shielded, no late repentance buys mercy, no heaven leans down to set things right. Out on the storm-struck heath, Lear loses crown and shelter and finally his reason, and the tempest outside is the smaller of the two. What makes the play unbearable is its refusal of consolation, the way it carries a father to the brink of seeing clearly only to take from him the one thing that recognition might have saved. Few works look so steadily at suffering and find the universe with nothing to say.

title: Stoner
author: John Edward Williams
extract: An occasional student who comes upon the name may wonder idly who William Stoner was, but he seldom pursues his curiosity beyond a casual question.
blurb: "That time of year thou mayst in me behold." A professor reads the sonnet aloud to a room of bored agriculture students, then stops and asks the farmer's son among them what it means, and though the boy cannot answer, something in him has already turned toward literature and will never turn back. William Stoner gives his life to that turning. He teaches without distinction, marries a woman who freezes him out of his own house, loses his daughter slowly to her mother, and finds one season of love he is forced to give up. The novel tells you in its first paragraph that he died obscure and was forgotten, his name nothing to the students who stumble on it. Then it spends three hundred plain, unhurried pages making you grieve him like your own father. Williams never raises his voice, and somehow each small defeat lands like a held breath finally released. You will see your own unlived life in his.

title: A Tomb for Boris Davidovich
author: Danilo Kiš
extract: I've reached my mature years—why spoil my biography?
blurb: They have already broken him: the lungs, the kidneys, the joints, his body a heap of sores under the rubber truncheons. Yet Boris Davidovich Novsky, old Bolshevik and fierce internationalist, will not sign. He does not fear death. He fears that the false confession his interrogator demands will become the only document to outlive him, and so corrupt forever the biography he spent forty years writing in his own blood. For two weeks the two men wrestle over the wording, each fighting for a single phrase, and Fedukin plays his cruelest card: every day Novsky refuses, another man is shot in his name. Kiš tells it as archival fact, a true story recovered from the footnotes of the Terror, and that dry documentary calm is what makes it unbearable. Few pages have caught so exactly the vanity and the grandeur of a man who would rather die than let his life be misread.

title: Zapovit (My Testament)
author: Taras Shevchenko
extract: When I am dead, then bury me In my beloved Ukraine, My tomb upon a grave mound high Amid the spreading plain,
blurb: Lay me in a high grave on the steppe, the poet asks, where my eyes can still watch the fields and my ears still hear the Dnieper roar. What begins as a dying man's wish for burial becomes, in twenty-four lines, the testament of a whole people. Shevchenko wrote Zapovit at thirty-one, gravely ill and half-convinced he was writing his own last words, and the poem turns from the tenderness of one grave to a command that still frightens tyrants: rise up, break your chains, water your freedom with the blood of the men who took it. Then it softens again, unbearably, into a single request. In the great new family of the free, remember me with a kind and quiet word. No poem is more beloved in Ukraine, second only to the anthem, set to music more than sixty times. To read it is to hear a country asking not to be forgotten.

title: In Cold Blood
author: Truman Capote
extract: The village of Holcomb stands on the high wheat plains of western Kansas.
blurb: On a November night in 1959, two men drove across the wheat plains of western Kansas toward a farmhouse they had never seen, acting on a cellmate's tip that the place held a safe full of cash. There was no safe. They cut the telephone wires, tied the Clutter family one by one, and shot all four through the head for a few dollars and a portable radio. Truman Capote read a few paragraphs in the newspaper, went out to Holcomb, and stayed six years. What he built, In Cold Blood, he called the nonfiction novel: every fact checked, every name real, yet written with the inwardness fiction allows, until the reader is carried straight through the locked door and into the mind of Perry Smith, the small, broken, oddly gentle man who pulled the trigger. By the end you grieve for killers whose guilt was never in doubt, and cannot quite forgive yourself for it. Capote could not finish the book until Smith and Hickock were hanged, and that long wait shadows every sentence he set down before it.

title: Hopscotch
author: Julio Cortázar
extract: Only in dreams, in poetry, in play do we sometimes arrive at what we were before we were this thing that, who knows, we are.
blurb: On the pavement a child tosses a pebble and hops, square by square, toward the one chalked Heaven at the top. Cortázar built a whole novel on that game. Hopscotch begins with two tables of contents: read it straight through and you hold one book; follow the second, leaping between chapters in a prescribed, looping order, gathering up the "expendable" passages most novels would cut, and the same pages become another book entirely, one that doubles back and will not end. In bohemian Paris, Horacio Oliveira loves La Maga and cannot do the single thing she does without effort, which is to simply be alive inside her own life. He has read every philosophy and still cannot reach the center of anything. That center is the square called Heaven: always one toss of the stone away, never landed on by thinking. To read this book is to play the game and feel, exhilarated and undone, how the search and the reading are the same hopeless, holy act.

title: Miss Julie
author: August Strindberg
extract: I have climbed to the top of a column and sit there without being able to tell how to get down again.
blurb: The count is away, the midsummer bonfire is burning in the yard, and his daughter has come down to the kitchen to dance with the servants. Julie tells the valet Jean a recurring dream: she has climbed to the top of a high column and cannot get down again, only longing to fall. Jean dreams the reverse, of lying beneath a tall tree he aches to climb. Two dreams, one falling and one rising, and Strindberg sets them loose in a single room over one unbroken night to grind against each other. He prefaced the play insisting his people were not types but living contradictions, half-noble and half-brutal by turns, and Julie and Jean prove him right at every line: she is never only the count's daughter, he is never only the boot-black. That is what makes the warm kitchen so dangerous. When the class line they cross snaps back into place, it falls on the one who had the farther height to lose, and the count's bell, ringing through the wall, settles the rest.

title: Faust
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
extract: My worthy friend, gray are all theories, and green alone Life's golden tree.
blurb: Goethe's scholar has read everything and feels nothing. He stands among his books at midnight, learned past all use and dead to the world, until the devil offers a bargain and Faust names stranger terms than the legend ever dared: not his soul outright, but a wager that no single moment will ever feel so perfect he begs it to stay. Mephistopheles takes the bet certain it will be easy. Across two parts and sixty years of writing, Goethe proves it is not. Part I narrows to one ruined girl, Gretchen, tender and doomed by the love Faust brings her. Part II opens onto everything at once: an emperor's court, ancient Greece, drowned land won back from the sea, a mind that cannot stop reaching. What it finally knows is the most generous claim literature ever dared, that to strive without rest, even into wreckage, is itself the thing worth saving. Gray are all theories, Goethe writes, and green alone life's golden tree.

title: Two Treatises of Government
author: John Locke
extract: The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges everyone, and reason, which is that law, teaches all mankind.
blurb: Before Locke, the question of why anyone should obey a king had a settled answer: God placed him there, and authority ran downhill from heaven to Adam to crown. The First Treatise takes that doctrine, in Robert Filmer's confident phrasing, and pulls it apart joint by joint. But the demolition only clears the ground. What Locke builds on it in the Second Treatise is one of the boldest claims any Englishman has set in print: that power runs the other way, upward, from people who entered the world already holding their lives, their liberty, their property, and who lend a government only as much authority as it takes to guard those things. Break the trust and the loan is called in. A people may dissolve a government that turns on them, not as rebels but as creditors. Read it and you are reading the words Jefferson would borrow, almost unchanged, when thirteen colonies decided their king had broken the trust and the loan was theirs to call in.

title: The Wings of the Dove
author: Henry James
day: The Wings of the Dove publication; 1902
extract: She waited, Kate Croy, for her father to come in.
blurb: Kate Croy and Merton Densher are in love and too poor to marry. Then Milly Theale arrives in London, an American girl with an immense fortune and, though almost no one says it aloud, very little time to spend it. Kate's plan is simple to state and unbearable to watch unfold: let Densher court the dying heiress, let her come to love him, and wait. Henry James wraps this cold arithmetic in such exquisite indirection, so much felt and so little spoken, that the cruelty surfaces only in glimpses, the way a face shifts behind a veil. His sentences circle their subject and qualify and withhold, until you understand that the evasions are the meaning, that everyone here is hiding from what they are doing. And Milly, called a dove for her sweetness, sees further than anyone credits her for. What she does with what she sees is the most generous and devastating turn in the book, and James gives it to you the way the others receive it, not in the moment but in the hush that follows.

title: The Threepenny Opera
author: Bertolt Brecht
extract: What is the robbing of a bank compared to the founding of a bank?
blurb: A street singer cranks a barrel organ and sings of a shark that shows its pretty teeth and of Macheath, who keeps his knife well out of sight, and within sixteen bars the most quoted tune of the century has slipped its moorings and walked off into the world on its own. That is the trick of The Threepenny Opera: Kurt Weill writes melodies so sweet your foot taps before your conscience catches up, and Brecht sets them to lyrics that name you, in your good seat, as the real thief. Mack the Knife runs his thieves by ledger and courtesy; Peachum licenses the city's beggars for a cut; the police chief is Macheath's oldest friend. What, the play asks, is robbing a bank beside founding one? When the king's messenger gallops in at the last second to pardon the murderer, Brecht points at the absurdity out loud, because in your life no such messenger comes. You leave humming the song anyway.

title: Letters to a Young Poet
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
extract: Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.
blurb: Are these any good? It is the question every beginner aches to have answered, and it is the one Rilke refuses, across all ten letters, ever to touch. Franz Kappus was nineteen, a military cadet who had mailed his verses to a poet barely older than himself, and what came back was not a verdict but a redirection. Go into yourself, Rilke tells him; find the hour of deepest quiet, the place where the need to write lives, and ask whether you would die if it were forbidden you. If the answer is no, then do not write. From there the letters keep widening, through solitude and doubt and the long work of love, toward the strange counsel at the book's heart: that a young man should be patient with everything unresolved inside him and learn to love the questions themselves rather than force them shut. Read them young and they quietly reset what you thought a life in art would cost. Few books have ever trusted a stranger so completely with his own becoming.

title: The Enchiridion
author: Epictetus
extract: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power.
blurb: Hold it in one hand and you have already grasped its first claim. The book is small, a manual a soldier could carry to war, and everything it asks turns on a single line drawn through a life. Some things are up to you; most are not. Your judgments, your desires, the use you make of whatever happens, these are yours. Your body, your reputation, the people you love, tomorrow morning, these never were. Epictetus learned the distinction the hard way, born a slave in Nero's Rome and lame for life, made to find the one thing no owner can reach. The sayings his student Arrian set down do not soothe; they reorganize a person from the inside, schooling desire away from what can be seized and toward what cannot. Come to it wanting consolation and it hands you something harder and far better instead: the small, unbreakable part of a life that was always only yours to keep.

title: First Love
author: Ivan Turgenev
extract: O youth, youth! little dost thou care for anything; thou art master, as it were, of all the treasures of the universe.
blurb: Zinaida is twenty-one and keeps a parlour of grown men circling her for sport, and into that court drifts the sixteen-year-old from the estate next door, ruined before he knows what has touched him. She is fond of him, which is worse than the teasing she hands the others, because fondness leaves him nothing to fight. Turgenev drew the novella from his own boyhood, and the wound is dressed with a son's exactness. Then a night by the garden wall shows Vladimir who Zinaida truly loves, and it is not a rival of his own age but his own father, elegant and remote, holding her in a register the boy cannot yet imagine. What the book understands is how love first arrives at full adult power, before anyone is ready to carry it. The whip-mark she lifts to her lips, tenderness chosen in the teeth of cruelty, is among the most precise images in nineteenth-century fiction.

title: Native Son
author: Richard Wright
extract: He was their property, heart and soul, body and blood; what they did claimed every atom of him, sleeping and waking
blurb: An alarm clock shrieks, and the first thing Bigger Thomas does that morning is corner a rat against the wall of the cramped one-room apartment his whole family shares, and bring it down with a hurled skillet. Hold the image, because the whole novel lives inside it. Richard Wright wrote the first book by a Black American to climb the bestseller lists, and he did it by refusing every comfort: Bigger kills a white girl, smothering her into silence in the dark because a Black man found in her bedroom is already a dead one. Wright will not let you condemn him cleanly or pity him cleanly, since both responses let you off the hook. Across three movements named "Fear," "Flight," and "Fate," the book insists that a country built to erase a man has left him violence as the only act that feels like choosing. The title is the charge: Bigger is America's native son, and the nation that raised him has no language for what it sees in the mirror.

title: Darkness at Noon
author: Arthur Koestler
extract: The cell door slammed behind Rubashov.
blurb: Through the wall of an unnamed Soviet prison, a Tsarist officer taps out messages in a code of knocks, and Nikolai Rubashov, who helped build the regime that has now jailed him, taps back. He is an Old Bolshevik arrested by his own revolution at four in the morning, and what unnerves him is not the prospect of death but that he cannot, after long searching, find the flaw in the case against him. The same arithmetic he once used to justify any cruelty for the cause is the arithmetic his interrogators turn on him now. Arthur Koestler wrote this after the Moscow show trials, when old revolutionaries confessed in open court to crimes no one believed they had done, and he set out to make that confession comprehensible from the inside. There is no torture here, only the cold advance of an argument toward its conclusion. The deadliest thing a man can surrender is the right to say I, and Rubashov long ago taught himself to call that word a grammatical fiction.

title: The Library of Babel
author: Jorge Luis Borges
extract: The universe (which others call the Library) is composed of an indefinite and perhaps infinite number of hexagonal galleries
blurb: Picture a library with no walls and no end: identical six-sided rooms repeating in every direction, each shelf holding books of exactly four hundred and ten pages, each page a lattice of the same twenty-five symbols. Borges asks one annihilating question. If the shelves hold every possible arrangement of those symbols, then somewhere on them sits every book that could ever be written: the true history of your death, the faithful catalogue of the whole Library, and a hundred thousand near-perfect lies that differ from the truth by a single comma. The men who live there once wept with joy at this, then went mad hunting for the one page that would justify their lives. What makes The Library of Babel unbearable and gorgeous is how it turns a mathematician's daydream into a portrait of us, small creatures adrift in a total order we cannot read. An old librarian, going blind a few galleries from where he was born, sets down one last conjecture, and for a held breath the dread of the place turns into something close to grace.

title: The Faerie Queene
author: Edmund Spenser
extract: Sleepe after toyle, port after stormie seas, Ease after warre, death after life does greatly please.
blurb: Despair, cornered in his cave, does not attack the knight. He reasons with him, and the reasoning is set to music so sweet it nearly works: Sleepe after toyle, port after stormie seas, Ease after warre, death after life does greatly please. That is the danger of The Faerie Queene. Its beauty is never decoration but a force that can save a soul or unmake one. Spenser built a land where every forest is a moral condition and every monster a sin given a body that bleeds and shrieks; in the first canto the monster Errour vomits books and frogs as she dies. He planned twelve books, one private virtue each, and finished six before death took the rest, and the half-built scale feels right: Gloriana, the queen the whole poem rides toward, keeps a court no knight reaches. Read it slowly, as the nine-line stanza insists, each closing on a long alexandrine that makes the ground itself resist being crossed. Milton studied this before Paradise Lost. The quest is the glory; the queen was never meant to arrive.

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
extract: In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind.
blurb: On a plain in La Mancha, a thin old man levels his lance at a row of windmills, certain they are giants with flailing arms, and charges. He is wrong, of course. He is wrong about almost everything: the roadside inn is a castle, the farm girl Dulcinea a princess, a barber's brass basin the golden helmet of a hero. He has read so many tales of knighthood that his mind has cracked open, and out of the crack pours something the saner world has lost. Beside him trots Sancho Panza, fat and proverb-stuffed and helplessly devoted, and theirs may be the tenderest friendship in all of literature. The miracle is that you start by laughing at the madman and end unable to laugh, because his delusion is only the wish that the world were braver and kinder than it is. No book is funnier, and few are this kind. Cervantes will not tell you whether to mock the knight or kneel to him, and by the end you cannot do either alone.

title: War and Peace
author: Leo Tolstoy
extract: Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now just family estates of the Buonapartes.
blurb: Natasha Rostova stands at the edge of her first ball, sixteen and terrified no one will ask her to dance, and Tolstoy gives the moment the same grave attention he gives the cannon at Borodino, because to him they are the same size. That is the secret of War and Peace: a girl's held breath and an empire's invasion belong to one continuous fabric of being alive. Five families move through fifteen years of Napoleonic war, and the book follows them so closely that you stop reading about them and simply live beside them, year after year. Prince Andrei lies wounded under a sky so high and endless that everything he believed about glory falls silent. Pierre, rich and adrift, keeps mistaking the shape of meaning and stumbling toward it anyway. Tolstoy's argument, woven into the structure itself, is that no general wins a battle: history is the sum of millions of frightened private wills, all moving at once. You finish it changed, the way you finish a decade.

title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
extract: I have possessed that heart, that noble soul, in whose presence I seemed to be more than I really was.
blurb: She is cutting bread for a crowd of younger brothers and sisters the first time Werther sees her, and that is all it takes: he loves Charlotte instantly, completely, hopelessly, for she is already promised to a steady and decent man named Albert. The whole novel is the letters Werther sends a friend, and you can almost watch his hand shake more with each one as the gap between the world he feels and the world that exists widens past bearing. Goethe poured the book out in six weeks at twenty-four, bleeding his own thwarted love for a real Charlotte into every line. What he discovered was a new kind of ruin: a soul undone not by anything life withholds but by the sheer excess of its own longing, a tenderness too vast for any ordinary day to hold. It made him famous overnight and made heartbreak fashionable; across Europe young men wept over it and dressed in Werther's blue coat and yellow waistcoat to follow their hero all the way down.

title: Women in Love
author: D.H. Lawrence
extract: Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen sat one morning in the window-bay of their father's house in Beldover.
blurb: Two men bolt the door, strip to the skin, and wrestle by firelight until neither can tell whose limbs are whose. Nothing is spoken; nothing needs to be. That scene carries the question Women in Love turns on: whether two people can come close enough to love without one of them consuming the other. Lawrence sets two couples against it. Ursula loves Rupert Birkin, who wants what he calls star-equilibrium, two separate selves held in orbit rather than the gravitational collapse he believes most love really is. Gudrun takes Gerald Crich, the mine owner who has never wanted anything except to own it outright, his collieries, his body, her. Desire here is weather, something that moves through people and wrecks them, and Lawrence trusts the texture of a single touch to say what his characters cannot. By the time the four climb into the Alps, the cold is already deciding which philosophy can survive being loved.

title: Sonnets from the Portuguese
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
extract: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
blurb: Count the ways. That instruction, from the most famous love poem in English, is usually mistaken for rapture, but read the whole sequence and you find something stranger and more moving: a woman counting because she cannot quite believe the sum. Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote these forty-four sonnets in a darkened Wimpole Street room during her courtship with Robert, an invalid who had long since folded away any expectation of being loved, and then was. She published them disguised as translations from the Portuguese, unable to claim such nakedness as her own. The sonnet had spent three centuries as a man's instrument, aimed at a silent, distant beloved; here it turns inward, and its subject is not longing but the slow, frightened work of trusting that the love will hold. Sonnet by sonnet she tests her disbelief against his constancy. By the forty-third she is not rhapsodising. She is counting, because she needs the total to come out true.

title: Robinson Crusoe
author: Daniel Defoe
extract: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family.
blurb: He cut a tall post into the sand and notched it once for every day, a calendar kept by a man with no one to keep time for. This is the texture of Daniel Defoe's island, and it turns out to be strangely gripping: a single castaway, a hatchet and some biscuit hauled from the wreck, and the slow, patient labour of staying alive and sane at once. Crusoe keeps a ledger of his blessings against his miseries in two neat columns, raises goats, learns after many failures to bake bread and fire a pot that will not crack. Defoe, who had himself been bankrupted and jailed, writes it all in the plain, unhurried voice of a ship's log, and makes the case that a self can be built the way a shelter is, plank by salvaged plank. Then, years in, a single bare footprint pressed into the sand, and the discovery that he is not alone frightens him more than the storm that wrecked him ever did.

title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
author: John Keats
extract: Beauty is truth, truth beauty,--that is all Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.
blurb: Carved on the urn, a lover bends toward a kiss that will never quite land; the girl he reaches for will never age out of being lovely, and the two will hang there, an inch apart, for as long as the marble holds. Ode on a Grecian Urn turns that frozen inch into its whole argument. The piper's melodies are sweeter for being unheard, the boughs sweeter for never shedding a leaf, because art rescues a moment from the decay that ruins everything it touches, and pays for the rescue by denying it fulfilment forever. Keats was twenty-three, already nursing the consumption that had taken his brother, and the consolation was not theoretical; he needed the beautiful thing to also be the true thing. When the urn at last speaks, telling us beauty is truth and truth beauty, hear it not as a neat moral but as a dying man refusing to let go of the only equation that might save him.

title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
extract: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
blurb: A handful of dust is all it takes. Polynices fell attacking his own city, and the new king of Thebes has ruled that the traitor's body stay above ground, food for the dogs and the noon sun, a punishment built to outlast death. His sister Antigone scatters dust over him anyway, sealing her fate in an act briefer than the sentence that describes it. What makes Sophocles' play unbearable is that neither of them is wrong. Antigone obeys the gods of the dead, who were old before any throne existed; Creon is holding a city together after civil war, and a king whose edicts mean nothing rules nothing. The play takes no side. It destroys them both and keeps Creon on stage long after the girl is walled alive into her rock tomb, so he can total what his principle has cost. Twenty-five centuries on, no one has untied the knot: the law of the city stands, and the city is empty of everyone worth saving.

title: Under the Volcano
author: Malcolm Lowry
extract: No se puede vivir sin amar. (One cannot live without loving.)
blurb: Mezcal in the morning, then more mezcal, and a mind so steeped it reads doom in everything: a torn travel poster, the two volcanoes standing over the town like sentries at the gate of the underworld. Geoffrey Firmin, a disgraced British Consul, drinks his way through a single Day of the Dead in Mexico while his estranged wife Yvonne, just returned, and his half-brother Hugh try to reach the man still alive somewhere inside the ruin. What makes the book unbearable is its lucidity. Firmin is never numb; he understands with awful precision the love being held out to him, and exactly why he cannot close his hand around it. Lowry's prose comes in great hallucinatory swells, Spanish and English and grief all braided together, and a ravine waits at the edge of town through every chapter. By the end you have watched a man read every omen gathering to kill him and choose, hour by lucid hour, not to be saved.

title: Ferdydurke
author: Witold Gombrowicz
extract: I felt that my form was being violated from outside and that I could do nothing about it.
blurb: Imagine waking adult and self-possessed, then watching a professor stroll into your room, click his tongue, and address you as a schoolboy, until the years peel away and your own face goes soft and stupid against your will. That is the morning Witold Gombrowicz hands his Józef, who spends the rest of the book being shrunk back into childhood by nothing more than what everyone around him expects. The horror is that it works. Gombrowicz had words for the machinery: gęba, the grimace a crowd presses onto you until it becomes your face, and pupa, the rump of an immaturity no one ever outgrows. He stages it everywhere, in a classroom where two boys fight an actual duel of grimaces, in a household weaponising its own modern youthfulness, in a country manor where courting a servant girl curdles into farce. The novel even turns on itself, breaking off into prefaces that quarrel with their own argument. Close it and you will never again be sure your personality is yours.

title: The Adventures of Augie March
author: Saul Bellow
extract: I am an American, Chicago born - Chicago, that somber city - and go at things as I have taught myself, free-style
blurb: Everyone in Augie March's Chicago has plans for him: the imperious Grandma Lausch, ruling the household of his nearly blind mother; the crippled, brilliant Einhorn, who runs the ward's loans and numbers from a wheelchair; Thea, who drives him to Mexico to hunt iguanas with a trained eagle. Saul Bellow called them "reality instructors," and the book is the long, joyous record of how each one recruits Augie and how each one loses him. What makes The Adventures of Augie March feel like a window thrown open is the voice: a high-low American speech that vaults from Heraclitus to street-corner patter inside one sentence, going at things, as Augie says, free-style. Bellow had written two careful, buttoned novels before this; here he let the language run, and American fiction was never quite so polite again. Augie never settles, never lets himself be completed, and the book never asks him to. Refusal, it turns out, is the freedom this whole rushing book is in love with.

title: Lord of the Flies
author: William Golding
extract: Ralph wept for the end of innocence, the darkness of man's heart, and the fall through the air of the true, wise friend called Piggy.
blurb: The conch shell summons them to assembly, a pink-and-cream trumpet that means whoever holds it may speak, and for a while it works. British schoolboys, marooned on a tropical island with no adult left to perform good behavior for, build a parliament, vote, keep a signal fire smoking against the empty horizon. Then Jack paints his face, and something older than the rules comes up through the paint. William Golding had taught boys in a classroom and commanded men at sea, and he knew what he was writing was not fantasy: the beast the children fear in the dark is not on the island at all, but in the chests of the hunters who go looking for it. What undoes you is the slowness, civilization peeling off one ritual at a time, the vote curdling into the hunt, the fire they need for rescue traded for the fire of the kill. By the end you understand why a sow's head on a stake, black with flies, is the only god this island can grow.

title: The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter
author: Carson McCullers
extract: In the town there were two mutes, and they were always together.
blurb: They come to him one at a time, and they tell him everything. A girl who hears whole symphonies no one else can hear, a Black doctor worn thin by a lifetime of injustice, a half-drunk agitator nobody else will listen to, the watchful man behind the café counter: each finds a way to John Singer, a deaf-mute in a small Georgia mill town, and pours out a life. They are certain he understands them, because he never tells them otherwise. Carson McCullers was twenty-three when she caught the cruellest thing about loneliness, that a silence we fill with our own longing can feel more like being heard than any answer ever could. And Singer, who holds the whole town's confidence, is himself in love with another mute shut away in a state asylum, a man who barely knows he is alive. The novel moves at the pace of a long Southern summer, gathering its quiet griefs without hurry. By the last page you see it plainly: everyone here is talking, tenderly, into a face that cannot answer back.

title: The Time Machine
author: H.G. Wells
extract: There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it.
blurb: Put a finger on a small brass lever, and watch the model wink out of the present like a soap bubble. That parlour trick, performed for a skeptical dinner party, is how The Time Machine begins, but the trick is the least of what Wells does. He sends his Traveller forward to the year 802,701, where the leisured classes have softened into the childlike Eloi who graze in the sunlight, and the workers have descended into the Morlocks, pale things in the dark who climb up at night to feed on them. That is the famous parable, and it is not the deepest thing here. The machine carries him further still, to a cold red beach beneath a swollen dying sun, where nothing stirs but a few crab-shaped horrors in the failing light. Wells understood before anyone that deep time does not honour our dramas; it swallows them. The Traveller comes back with two white flowers a dead girl pressed into his pocket, the only proof he ever held anything at all.

title: The Odyssey
author: Homer
extract: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
blurb: A goddess offers a man immortality on an island where nothing can ever harm him, and every evening he sits on the shore and weeps, staring out at the water toward a rocky little kingdom and a wife who has aged ten years without him. That refusal is the secret heart of The Odyssey: not whether Odysseus can outwit the Cyclops or sail past the Sirens, but whether an ordinary mortal life, brief and grief-prone, is worth more than never dying at all. Homer gives us not the warrior at Troy but the strategist at the end of his patience, a man who survives by thinking faster than any god expects, who even walks into the land of the dead to ask the way home. When he reaches Ithaca at last he announces nothing. He bends a bow no one else can string and kills every man who has been eating his food and courting his wife. The cunning that took Troy and the cunning that takes back a house are the same cunning, and the poem knows it.

title: To Autumn
author: John Keats
extract: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, close bosom-friend of the maturing sun.
blurb: Where are the songs of Spring? Keats poses the question near the end and then, almost tenderly, tells himself not to go looking. To Autumn came in September 1819, after he walked the harvested fields outside Winchester, ground he wrote he had never liked so well as that month. It is the last of his great odes and the only one that does not strain to be elsewhere: the Nightingale longs to dissolve into the dark and the Grecian Urn climbs off into cold philosophy, but autumn keeps both feet in the stubble. The first stanza loads the vines until they bend, the second lays the season down asleep on a half-reaped furrow, and the third gathers the choir that is left, the small gnats mourning in the willows, the full-grown lambs bleating from the hills, the swallows massing for a sky they are about to leave. He was twenty-three and had seventeen months to live, and still he does not flinch. The poem simply notices that ripeness and ending are one weather, and chooses to stay out in it.

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
extract: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
blurb: Out across the dark water a single green light burns at the end of a dock, and on the lawn opposite a man stands alone, arms stretched toward it, trembling. Jay Gatsby throws enormous parties for hundreds of strangers and drifts through none of them; the whole gold-lit machine exists to summon back one woman he loved in Louisville five years gone, who married old money while he was away at the war. The wonder of the book is that Gatsby chases not a future but a past already polished past anything the living Daisy could ever be, and Fitzgerald sees clean through to the ruin in it: Tom and Daisy are careless people who break things and retreat into their wealth, and the green light was never a place to arrive at, only a direction to keep facing. And then there are the sentences. Read the last page aloud, feel the current take you, boats borne back ceaselessly into the past, and try to set the book down.

title: The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
extract: I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire.
blurb: The title comes from the blackest speech in Macbeth, the one about a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing, and Faulkner takes it literally. The novel opens inside the mind of Benjy Compson, who cannot tell this morning from thirty years past, for whom his sister Caddy survives only as the smell of trees and an ache he has no words to hold. The same ruin of one Southern family is then told again, and again, and again: by Quentin, drowning in time at Harvard; by Jason, mean and grasping; and at last by Dilsey, the Black servant who endures because she never believed the Compson name was worth a thing. To read it is to climb out of Benjy's dark, mind by mind, into the still light of Dilsey's Easter morning. And at the centre of every voice stands Caddy, the lost girl her brothers circle and none can keep, whom the novel itself loves too much to ever let speak for herself.

title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
author: T.S. Eliot
extract: I have measured out my life with coffee spoons;
blurb: Let us go then, you and I: the poem opens like an invitation, the evening spread above the half-deserted streets like a patient etherised upon a table. What follows is the inner weather of a man circling one overwhelming question he cannot bring himself to ask, deferring it past the toast and the tea, past the women who come and go talking of Michelangelo, until the asking has become impossible. Every reader who has stood at a doorway polishing the perfect sentence and then walked away having said nothing recognises him exactly. It is built almost entirely of dread: the thinning hair noticed by others, the coffee spoons in which a whole life is measured out, the eternal Footman holding the coat and snickering. T.S. Eliot wrote it barely out of his early twenties and somehow already knew how a self can congeal into gesture. The verse that opened modern poetry ends among mermaids singing far out at sea, a music he is certain is not for him, and the soft horror of waking into the ordinary and going under.

title: I and Thou
author: Martin Buber
extract: All real living is meeting.
blurb: There is a difference between saying 'You' to someone and saying 'It,' and Martin Buber built a whole philosophy on it. To speak 'Thou' is to stand before another in full presence, holding nothing back, so that a person, a tree, even God stops being a thing you observe and becomes a whole world that meets you back. To speak 'It' is to step away and describe, measure, use. These are not passing moods but two ways of having a self, and Buber's quiet, shattering claim is that the I who says 'Thou' is not the same I who says 'It.' He writes in prose so compressed it reads like scripture, mourning a modern life that has let usefulness swallow encounter, until even the people we love thin into functions. God he calls the eternal Thou, the one relation that can never curdle into an object. Every other Thou, he admits, will. I and Thou lives in the brief warm interval before it does, and it will leave you desperate to keep one bond from going cold.

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
author: Milan Kundera
extract: The heaviest of burdens crushes us, we sink beneath it, it pins us to the ground.
blurb: Lightness should be a relief, yet the title calls it unbearable, and the novel spends itself earning that contradiction. Milan Kundera begins with a thought borrowed from Nietzsche: if each moment comes only once and never returns, it leaves no mark and costs nothing, so a life lived entirely without weight slowly floats free of meaning. Tomas, a Prague surgeon who has arranged his affairs so that no woman can claim him, takes this weightlessness for freedom, until Tereza turns up in his city with a book under her arm, falls ill on his sofa, and will not leave. The gravity of loving her is unlike anything he has carried. The Soviet tanks of 1968 force the same question onto a whole country, showing what becomes of a private life when history arrives without knocking. Kundera tells you early how these lovers will end, so suspense drains away and only the ache remains: that to refuse all weight is to vanish, and to love anyone fully is to hand them the power to break you.

title: The Tell-Tale Heart
author: Edgar Allan Poe
extract: True! Nervous, very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
blurb: Listen to how calmly he explains it. Edgar Allan Poe's narrator wants nothing but to prove he is sane, and so he walks you through it with the patience of a man who has rehearsed: how for seven nights he eased a lantern's thread of light across a sleeping old man's face, waiting for the one pale, filmed vulture eye to open. He killed for the eye, not the man. He buried the body beneath the floorboards and sat the arriving police directly above it, easy and victorious. The whole story is a confession the narrator mistakes for an explanation, and every protest of his clear mind only tightens the proof against him. Then he begins to hear it: a low, quick beating he cannot silence, swelling under the boards until it fills the room, the house, his skull. The Tell-Tale Heart knows the oldest terror is the one you carry inside you, growing louder the harder you pretend not to hear.

title: Beowulf
author: Anonymous
extract: LO, praise of the prowess of people-kings of spear-armed Danes, in days long sped, we have heard, and what honor the athelings won!
blurb: Out of the fog-bound moors, where the black mere boils under twisted roots, a shape comes walking toward the lighted hall: Grendel, who cannot bear the sound of men singing and means to silence it tooth by tooth. Against him stands a young warrior who strips off mail and sword to meet the monster bare-handed, because honour will have it no other way. The poem hammers forward on the old alliterative line, two beats and a breath, two beats and a breath, a meter built to be spoken aloud over a fire while the wind worries at the door. There are three fights, each lonelier than the last, and the last sends a grey king alone into a dragon's barrow while his companions slink up the hill. What survives is not the gold, buried cursed beside him, but the grief. Beowulf, the oldest long poem in English, already mourns the brave, doomed world that made it, and sings it into the dark anyway.

title: Death of a Salesman
author: Arthur Miller
extract: Attention must be paid.
blurb: He comes home early, the two sample cases too heavy, unable to keep the car on the road because his mind keeps sliding into a sunlit past that may never have happened. Willy Loman has sold things his whole life on one article of faith: that to be well-liked is to be worth something, that personality is capital you can bank against the future. Arthur Miller folds time so that a long-dead hotel-room scene presses through the wall of the present, until you cannot tell what Willy did from what he needed to believe he did. He has staked not only his own dignity but his sons' on a self the world refuses to honour, and his wife, watching him unravel, says the line that holds the whole play upright: attention must be paid. Miller's enormous claim is that this tired drummer, who drove the same New England roads for thirty years, earns the stature of tragedy. The grief is not that Willy fails, but that he believed, to the last, in the thing that was failing him.

title: The Shahnameh
author: Ferdowsi
extract: I suffered during these thirty years, but I have revived Iran with the Persian language.
blurb: For thirty years Ferdowsi wrote in a Persian he scoured clean of the Arabic that had arrived with conquest, raising a poem the size of a library to house a civilization that had already vanished. The Shahnameh runs from the world's first king to the fall of the last, generation upon generation of kings and heroes, and it has served ever since as the memory Iran keeps of itself. Its great engine is a terrible symmetry: the mightiest are undone not by enemies but from within, the ruin always cut to the exact measure of the gift. Nowhere does this land harder than when Rostam, the unbeaten champion of the age, fights a young warrior who has crossed a continent to find the father he never knew, and learns whose blood is on his hands only as the boy dies. Because the empire it exalts was ash when Ferdowsi began, every blaze of glory arrives already shadowed by its end. The poem mourns the very thing it sings.

title: Berlin Alexanderplatz
author: Alfred Döblin
extract: He stood outside the gates of Tegel Penitentiary, a free man.
blurb: Tram numbers, weather bulletins, the day's cattle prices from the slaughterhouse, a hymn, a headline about a killing three streets over: all of it pours into the prose without warning, because this is what Berlin actually sounded like in the late 1920s, and Alfred Döblin refused to turn the volume down. Through that din walks Franz Biberkopf, newly out of Tegel prison and sworn to himself that this time he will stay decent. The city has other plans. It pulls him back among thieves, takes an arm, takes the woman he loves and cannot protect, and grinds his small vow so fine that Death itself steps forward to speak with him. What makes the book unforgettable is that Döblin found a form not for the city but as the city: the same relentless material that batters Franz batters the reader on every page. You finish it knowing exactly how it feels to be one man against a place that does not pause for you.

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
extract: Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul.
blurb: "Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins." That is how a child rapist asks you to fall in love with him, and the horror of Nabokov's novel is how nearly it works. Humbert Humbert, a cultivated European with a gift for the perfect phrase, narrates his years of preying on a twelve-year-old girl in English so voluptuous you catch yourself savouring a sentence before you remember what it is confessing. The prose is not a frame around the crime; it is the crime's silk disguise, the means by which Dolores Haze is talked out of the room while a creature called "Lolita" is invented to replace her. But she keeps surfacing anyway: the girl crying herself to sleep in roadside motels, the child who had a life before this man found her. To read it is to be seduced and then to feel the seduction curdle in your hands, which is exactly what Nabokov built it to do.

title: Cathedral
author: Raymond Carver
extract: My eyes were still closed. I was in my house. I knew that. But I didn't feel like I was inside anything.
blurb: Late in the evening, after the wine and the dope and the talk have wound down, a blind man named Robert lays his hand over the narrator's and tells him to keep drawing. They are making a cathedral on the side of a grocery bag, because a program flickering on the television has left the narrator unable to say what a cathedral even is. He is a small, fortified man, jealous of the long correspondence his wife kept with this blind friend, contemptuous of a closeness he has never managed himself. Raymond Carver writes him in flat, declarative sentences, each one another brick in the wall. And then, eyes shut, pencil still moving under another man's hand, the wall is simply not there. Carver never names what opens. He trusts a moving pencil and two hands to carry what this marriage's words never could, and you feel the room go quiet around it.

title: The Half-Finished Heaven
author: Tomas Tranströmer
extract: Each man is a half-open door leading to a room for everyone.
blurb: Despondency stops mid-stride. Anguish stops. Even the vulture, wheeling overhead, breaks off its flight, and into that sudden stillness a light comes streaming, so bright the ghosts themselves stoop to take a drink. This is the strange, exalted weather of Tomas Tranströmer's title poem, fourteen lines in which fear simply lifts and the world stands revealed. Cave paintings surface from the ice-age dark. Strangers walk together in the sun by the hundred. And then the line people carry around for the rest of their lives: each person is a half-open door, leading to a room for everyone. Tranströmer worked as a psychologist among juvenile prisoners and the broken, and he writes grace the way a physician writes a diagnosis, plainly, without a flourish, so you believe it. The heaven of the title is unfinished, still being built. But for the length of this poem the door swings open, the lake becomes a window into the earth, and you are let inside.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
extract: During the whole of a dull, dark, and soundless day in the autumn of the year, when the clouds hung oppressively low in the heavens.
blurb: Approach the house and the first wrong thing is its reflection: the grey, decaying mansion sits perfectly doubled in the black tarn below it, as though a second House of Usher were already waiting underwater for the first to come down. Poe is the writer who discovered that dread can be built before anything happens, that a low sky and a vacant eye-like window and a barely visible crack running from roof to foundation can work so deep into a reader's nerves that the eventual horror feels like recognition rather than surprise. Inside, Roderick Usher trembles with a sensitivity so acute that light, sound, and his own pulse have become torture, while his twin sister Madeline fades toward a death that will not stay a death. The story's terrible insight is that a family and the walls it has never left can fuse into one organism and rot as one. By the last page you understand the crack was never only in the stone.

title: Poem of the End
author: Marina Tsvetaeva
extract: In this most Christian of worlds all poets are Jews.
blurb: They are walking to say goodbye, and they both know it. Poem of the End moves through the streets of Prague at the pace of two people prolonging the last hour of a love, past lit windows and over a bridge above the Vltava, toward the place where parting stops being a word and becomes a thing the body does. Tsvetaeva wrote it at thirty-one, exiled from a Russia that no longer existed, so the breakup carries a second loss folded inside it: the end of a person and the end of a home, mourned in one breath. Read it aloud and you hear love coming apart in the grammar itself, lines snapped to a gasp, exclamations splitting sentences down the middle, the whole poem stumbling forward like someone who cannot stop walking toward something irreversible. By the last crossing, the world that needed two people to hold it up simply lets go.

title: Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night
author: Dylan Thomas
day: World Hospice and Palliative Care Day
extract: Rage, rage against the dying of the light.
blurb: Four times the same command returns, each time harder than the last: Rage, rage against the dying of the light. Dylan Thomas built that insistence into the bones of the poem by choosing the villanelle, a nineteen-line form on two rhymes whose refrains are forced to recur whether the poet wills them or not. He turned the constraint into a son's argument with death. Across the stanzas he gathers wise men, good men, wild men and grave men, each finding at life's end some reason to resist the dark, until the catalogue narrows to one bed and one face: a father going blind and losing his voice, on what the poem calls the sad height. It does not mourn so much as command. The strangest of love letters, it is a son ordering his dying father not to leave gently but to rage, to curse and bless him with fierce tears, because watching the light go out quietly is the one thing he cannot bear, and the form itself makes that refusal say itself over and over.

title: The Bell Jar
author: Sylvia Plath
extract: I saw my life branching out before me like the green fig tree in the story.
blurb: There is a fig tree in this book, and on every branch a different life Esther Greenwood might choose: a husband, a book of poems, a professorship, a string of lovers in far-off countries. She sits starving beneath it, unable to reach for one without watching the others blacken and drop, so she chooses nothing while the whole tree rots above her head. Sylvia Plath drew Esther's prize summer at a New York fashion magazine, and the slow airless descent that follows, from her own hospitalization a decade before she wrote it, and published it under another name. What makes it almost unbearable is the clarity: Esther's wit never dulls and her eye never blurs, so the reader watches a first-rate mind narrate its own vanishing with terrible composure. The bell jar is her word for the glass that lowers over a life, where you breathe the same stale air and look out and cannot, however hard you reach, touch the world on the other side.

title: Fragment 31
author: Sappho
extract: Peer of gods he seemeth to me, the blissful Man who sits and gazes at thee before him,
blurb: Equal to the gods, she calls the man who gets to sit across from the one she loves and simply listen to her talk. That is the whole wound: not his presence but his composure, the ordinary luck of a body that can hear that laughter and stay intact. Sappho's body cannot. The poem becomes a catalogue of her own collapse, taken down symptom by symptom as it happens, the tongue gone silent, a thin fire racing under the skin, the eyes blind, the ears roaring, sweat, trembling, a pallor greener than grass, and then the line that has outlived empires, that she is a little short of dying. No one had ever written desire this way before, from inside the falling body, and almost no one has done it better since. The poem breaks off mid-breath, the papyrus torn, the voice cut where the symptoms have already finished their work, and across twenty-six centuries you can still feel the room tilt.

title: Wide Sargasso Sea
author: Jean Rhys
extract: They say when trouble comes close ranks, and so the white people did. But we were not in their ranks.
blurb: "Our garden was large and beautiful as that garden in the Bible," Antoinette says of the estate where she was raised, "but it had gone wild." She is a white Creole girl on a Jamaica that has just freed the people her family once enslaved, hated by the Black islanders for what her name means and scorned by the English who come to buy what is left of it. Jean Rhys, born in Dominica, wrote Wide Sargasso Sea to give a country, a childhood, and a sanity to the woman Charlotte Brontë left raving in an attic: the first Mrs Rochester, the madwoman of Jane Eyre. The Englishman Antoinette marries is never named here. He renames her Bertha, carries her across the ocean to a cold locked room, and calls the result madness. Rhys calls it a sentence, handed down by empire and by marriage, and her prose holds you in the wide warm sea between her island and his England, so lush and disorienting you feel the ground soften and give way.

title: Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?
author: Edward Albee
extract: Who's afraid of Virginia Woolf? I am, George. I am.
blurb: Two in the morning, the faculty party long over, and George and Martha are still at it, drinks in hand, having trapped a younger couple on the sofa as audience and ammunition. He teaches history at the small New England college her father runs; she is louder, crueller, more wounded than anyone in the room but him. Edward Albee arms them with a whole vocabulary of blood sport, games with names, Humiliate the Host, Get the Guests, played with the awful fluency of two people who have no gentler language left between them. What makes the night unbearable is not the savagery but what it is for: only someone who has loved you for twenty years knows the precise place to set the knife, and that terrible accuracy is its own form of tenderness. Beneath every round runs a single story the two of them built and swore never to speak aloud. And the title, that drunken little song they keep humming, asks the only question the play truly cares about: who is afraid to live without the lie?

title: Eichmann in Jerusalem
author: Hannah Arendt
extract: The lesson of the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.
blurb: He sat in a bulletproof glass booth in a Jerusalem courtroom, and the woman sent to watch him kept waiting for the monster to surface. Adolf Eichmann had organized the trains that carried millions to the death camps, yet on the stand he produced only officialese and stock phrases, a man who seemed unable to think a single thought that was his own. From those weeks Hannah Arendt drew the most disquieting idea of the century: that the machinery of mass murder can run not on towering hatred but on the simple refusal to think, what she called the banality of evil. She does not shrink his guilt or the scale of the dead; she insists, harder, that he was ordinary, that the capacity was clerical, and that this should frighten us more than any demon would. The cost to her was savage; her account of the Jewish councils' cooperation broke friendships she would defend for the rest of her life. The book's enduring terror is that it never lets you set this man apart from yourself.

title: The Aeneid
author: Virgil
extract: I sing of arms and the man.
blurb: In a temple in Carthage, Aeneas finds the fall of Troy painted on the walls, his own dead among the figures, and weeps before strangers. Virgil gives the moment the line every Latin student carries: sunt lacrimae rerum, there are tears at the heart of things. That grief is the poem's engine. Aeneas is the founder of Rome and the most unwilling hero the ancient world made, dragged by pietas, that untranslatable fusion of duty, piety, and love, away from all he wants toward a future he will not live to see. He carries his old father from the flames and loses his wife in the smoke. He loves Dido, leaves her at the gods' command, and the leaving kills her. Descending among the dead in Book Six, he watches his father summon the unborn souls of Rome, emperors marched past a man who will never reach the city they build. No epic before it had grasped this: empire and a broken heart can be the same thing, and Rome is bought with all its founder must surrender.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
extract: There is only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is not being talked about.
blurb: A single sentence can ruin a life, and Wilde proves it. Lord Henry Wotton lays out his glittering creed in a Chelsea garden, that youth is the only thing worth having and beauty the only truth, and a beautiful young man who has never owned a thought of his own takes every word as gospel. Dorian stands before his finished portrait and wishes that the picture might grow old in his place, and the picture obliges. He moves through decades of pleasure, betrayal, and worse without a line on his face, while the canvas locked in the attic curdles into something monstrous, the one honest record of his soul. The genius is that Lord Henry, who commits no sin himself, is the most corrupting presence in every room; his epigrams are the pleasure of the book and its slow poison, the same wit Wilde performed in drawing rooms and here puts quietly on trial. Beauty without consequence sounds like the finest of bargains, right up until you climb to the attic and see what it has cost.

title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
author: Anonymous
extract: He who has seen everything, I will make known to the lands.
blurb: For seven days Gilgamesh would not bury his friend. He sat beside Enkidu's body, waiting for him to wake, and only when a worm fell from the dead man's face did the king of Uruk understand what death was. He had been two-thirds divine, terrifying, a tyrant who took the brides of his city on their wedding nights, until the gods shaped Enkidu from clay to be his match, and the two men fought and then loved each other like brothers. Now Gilgamesh runs. He crosses the desert in lion-skins, passes the scorpion-guardians of the mountains, rows across the waters of death to reach the one man who survived the flood and was granted life without end. He even finds the plant that restores youth, falls asleep beside a pool, and lets a serpent eat it. He comes home with nothing but the walls of his city. The oldest written story in the world was already about the only thing no power can buy: more time with the people we cannot keep.

title: Dangerous Liaisons
author: Pierre Choderlos de Laclos
extract: It is not enough to possess her, she shall give herself up.
blurb: In one of the most famous letters in the book, Valmont composes a love note to the devout Madame de Tourvel while lying with a courtesan, using her body as his writing desk, each pious phrase doubling as a lewd joke the woman he is courting will never catch. That is Dangerous Liaisons in miniature: a war fought entirely on paper, where seduction is a military campaign and tenderness is only another feint. Laclos, an artillery officer who wrote only this one novel, lets the letters do the damage; sincerity and its counterfeit grow impossible to tell apart, even by the people writing them. Valmont sets out to ruin Tourvel as a proof of skill and is genuinely undone by her, unable to find the line between his performance and his heart. The Marquise de Merteuil is the colder, finer mind, a woman who forged her intelligence into a blade because her century handed her nothing else to hold. They believe they are the players. The letters they cannot stop writing are the trap.

title: Pale Fire
author: Vladimir Nabokov
extract: I was the shadow of the waxwing slain by the false azure in the windowpane.
blurb: Pale Fire opens with a waxwing dead against a windowpane, the first line of a 999-line poem John Shade wrote in the last weeks of his life. Then the poem ends, Shade is shot in his own garden, and the book hands itself to Charles Kinbote, the neighbour who claims the poem secretly tells his story: that he is the exiled king of a far northern land called Zembla. His foreword, his line-by-line commentary, even his index become the vehicle for a tale Shade never wrote and may never have heard. To read it you must flip between the elegy and the gloss, watching a grieving father's quiet poem about his drowned daughter get colonised by a lonely madman's gorgeous, impossible romance. Nabokov makes the act of reading itself the plot, and turns a set of footnotes into one of the funniest, saddest novels ever built. Shade is gone by the second page. What survives is the argument over what he meant.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
extract: Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia was to remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice.
blurb: Ice arrives in Macondo like a holy relic, and a father pays to let his sons press their hands against the burning cold of it. That is the key to the whole book: here the marvelous is reported with the flat calm of weather, while the ordinary stuns. A girl rises into the sky while folding sheets and no one thinks to doubt it; a cloud of yellow butterflies trails a man wherever he goes; rain falls for years and then simply stops. Gabriel García Márquez follows seven generations of the Buendía family through a town they raised out of swamp, sons named Aureliano and José Arcadio circling back to the same loves and the same loneliness, as if the family were not living forward but turning in place. What the book is really about is solitude, the kind that runs in the blood and that no marriage and no war could ever cure. Read the last pages and you will understand, too late and forever, why the wind was always coming.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
extract: Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
blurb: For no reason he can ever name, a sailor lifts his crossbow and kills the white bird that had followed the ship through the Antarctic fog, and everything after is the price. The wind dies, the ship hangs as idle as a painted ship upon a painted ocean, water on every side and not a drop to drink. Coleridge wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner in the diction of an old medieval ballad, and it still moves like a fever you cannot wake from. The crew hang the albatross around his neck; then two hundred of them die and leave him alone with the corpses under a staring moon. What finally breaks the curse is not prayer or penance but an involuntary jolt of wonder, the moment he watches the water snakes coil and flash and blesses them without meaning to. And even then the tale is never done: doomed to wander and retell it, he stops a stranger on the way to a wedding, holds him with a glittering eye, and you, reading, cannot leave.

title: Nightwood
author: Djuna Barnes
extract: Life is not to be told, call it as loud as you like, it will not tell itself.
blurb: Nora Flood comes to Doctor Matthew O'Connor in the small hours and begs him to tell her everything he knows about the night, and the old fraud, an unlicensed gynaecologist in a wig and a soiled nightgown, talks until the light comes. He is talking her through grief. She has lost Robin Vote, the somnambule who drifts through these pages like a beast still half learning to be human, adored by everyone and held by no one. Djuna Barnes wrote one woman's obsession with another in a baroque, incantatory splendour T. S. Eliot set beside Elizabethan tragedy, prose so dense with image you stop and read a sentence twice for the dark shine of it. This is what it is to love something that cannot love you back and will not be kept, told in a register nearer prophecy than confession. It ends where such love goes, somewhere below speech and below the human, and Barnes lets you feel the descent coming long before it arrives.

title: Molloy
author: Samuel Beckett
extract: I am in my mother's room. It's I who live there now.
blurb: Sixteen stones, four pockets, and a tramp working out the one system that lets him suck each in strict rotation before any stone comes round twice. It is the funniest passage about despair you will ever read, and it tells you everything: Molloy brings flawless logic to the only problem small enough to solve, because the large ones, his failing legs, his abandoned bicycle, the riddle of how he ended up in his mother's room, have long since beaten him. Samuel Beckett lets a mind narrate its own coming apart, contradicting itself, walking back what it said, confessing the account is unreliable while setting it down anyway. Then a second voice begins, Moran, a tidy and pitiless man sent to find him, and the dread arrives quietly: he leaves whole and returns ruined, speaking in the cadences of the thing he hunted. By the end you cannot say where one man stops and the other starts, only that the rain on the glass may not be rain, the hour may not be the hour, and the voice goes on regardless.

title: Lysistrata
author: Aristophanes
extract: No wild beast is there, no flame of fire, more fierce and untameable than woman; the panther is less savage and shameless.
blurb: Twenty years into a war that has buried a generation, the women of Athens and Sparta decide to end it themselves, with the only leverage left to people who cannot vote or fight: they will refuse their husbands the marriage bed until the killing stops. They swear the oath over a shared bowl of wine, seize the treasury on the Acropolis, and wait. What follows is the frankest comedy of desire ever staged, husbands hobbling about in visible agony, a truce finally haggled out over the body of a naked girl who stands in for the map of Greece. But Aristophanes wrote it while Athens was bleeding itself white in a war it would go on to lose, and the laughter carries a wound: the suspicion that the people who pay for the slaughter are the only ones with any reason to stop it. Bawdy, furious, and tender about the ordinary life that war devours, it hands the whole catastrophe of empire to the people history never thought to ask.

title: Disgrace
author: J.M. Coetzee
extract: For a man of his age, fifty-two, divorced, he has, to his mind, solved the problem of sex rather well.
blurb: It begins with a sentence of chilling self-satisfaction: a man of fifty-two, divorced, who believes he has solved the problem of sex rather well. David Lurie, a Romantics professor in Cape Town, seduces a student, refuses the repentance his hearing demands, and is cast out of his comfortable life. He retreats to his daughter Lucy's smallholding in the Eastern Cape, where a far greater violence arrives and leaves none of his certainties standing. Coetzee writes in prose so cold and exact it works like a scalpel, refusing to tell the reader how to feel even as it makes Lurie's blindness to the people around him impossible to ignore. Power in post-apartheid South Africa is shifting, and every structure that once made a man like him untouchable dissolves beneath his feet. By the close he is carrying the bodies of dead dogs from a welfare clinic with a care he never managed toward a single living person, and the book will not let you mistake it for redemption.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
day: The Remains of the Day wins Booker; 1989
extract: The evening's the best part of the day. You've done your day's work. Now you can put your feet up and enjoy it.
blurb: Downstairs, Stevens pours brandy for the gentlemen of Europe while his father lies dying in an attic room, and he will remember it, without irony, as the proudest evening of his career.
