That is the whole tragedy of Stevens, butler of Darlington Hall, in miniature: a man who poured himself so completely into the ideal of service that there was nothing left over for grief, or for Miss Kenton, the housekeeper he loved in the only language he allowed himself, which was no language at all. Now, motoring west through the English countryside on the pretext of asking her back, he narrates his life as a ledger of dignity well kept, and the more carefully he balances it the more clearly we see what it cost. Kazuo Ishiguro writes Stevens's prose as the very instrument of his repression, each qualifying clause a door closing softly. By the time a stranger on a pier tells him the evening is the best part of the day, the ache is unbearable, because for Stevens the evening is nearly all that remains.

title: Birthday Letters
author: Ted Hughes
extract: But the jewel you lost was blue.
blurb: For more than three decades Ted Hughes said nothing while the world decided who he was: the husband who left, the man the suicide pointed back toward, the keeper of Sylvia Plath's silenced voice. Then, months before his own death, he broke that silence in the strangest way imaginable, not with a defence but with a direct address, eighty-eight poems spoken to Plath herself as though she might still answer. He does not argue. He reaches back past the myth her death had hardened into and finds the actual hours: a borrowed room, a colour she could not stop seeing, the weather of a marriage before its ending swallowed everything else. The present tense keeps her reachable, alive on the page, walking toward a February no poem will name. To read it is to overhear a conversation thirty-five years held in, finally said aloud to someone who can no longer hear it.

title: Brideshead Revisited
author: Evelyn Waugh
extract: I should like to bury something precious in every place where I've been happy.
blurb: Two undergraduates lie in the long grass under the elms, a bottle of cool golden wine beside the wild strawberries, and one of them carries a teddy bear named Aloysius and treats Oxford as a garden made only for pleasure. That summer is the bright lie at the heart of Evelyn Waugh's novel, because Charles Ryder is telling all of it backward, as a middle-aged officer billeted in the requisitioned house years later, and the beauty arrives already shadowed by its own loss. Brideshead is a great Catholic family scattering from its faith through drink and exile and unhappy marriage, and the deeper argument is that grace works like a fisherman's line: a twitch upon the thread can pull a soul home from the ends of the earth. Charles loves the place, loves Sebastian, then loves his sister, and is granted neither. What makes the house unbearably lovely is the same thing that makes it impossible to keep.

title: Satantango
author: László Krasznahorkai
extract: One morning near the end of October, not long before the first drops of the mercilessly long autumn rains began to fall.
blurb: Bells are ringing somewhere out past the rain, though the only chapel for miles is a roofless ruin with no bell, and no one on the dying estate can say what they hear. It has been raining for weeks; the mud is rising; the last villagers are plotting to slip away with a year's communal wages when word arrives that Irimiás is walking back up the road, the swindler they thought long dead. Krasznahorkai makes him a false messiah and the village a congregation so starved for rescue it will follow anyone who promises a door out of the muck. The prose moves the way the mud does, immense unbroken paragraphs that run for pages without letting you surface, until reading becomes weather you are caught inside. The shape is a tango, six chapters out and six chapters back, closing where it opened. At its still center a small forgotten girl poisons her cat and then herself, and the book never recovers, nor should it. The great novel of waiting to be saved and being fleeced instead.

title: The Cantos
author: Ezra Pound
extract: What thou lovest well remains, the rest is dross.
blurb: Open The Cantos at any page and it comes at you in pieces: a line of Greek, a Chinese character set whole into the margin, a snatch of Provençal song, a banker's ledger, the names of American founders. Ezra Pound spent nearly fifty years building this, calling it "a poem containing history," and he meant the whole of it, dynasties and usury and myth crammed into one fracturing verse. The center is Pisa, 1945, where he wrote eleven cantos from memory in a US Army cage while awaiting trial for treason, and where the vast machine turns suddenly, achingly tender: "What thou lovest well remains, the rest is dross." The poem never resolves. Near the end he writes "I cannot make it cohere," then two lines later insists "it coheres all right." He lets both stand. That refusal to tidy the wreckage is the truest thing a man ever made who tried to hold the entire world in his hands and could not put one piece of it down.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
extract: It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.
blurb: On a dreary night of November, a being's dull yellow eye opens for the first time, and the man who built it bolts from the room in terror of his own success. Everything in Mary Shelley's novel turns on that flight. Begun when she was eighteen, during a rain-locked Geneva summer where Byron had set ghost stories as a parlour game, Frankenstein outgrew the competition and became the first true work of science fiction. Its creature is no lurching brute: he teaches himself to read from Milton and Plutarch and Goethe, reasons his way to a full understanding of how completely he has been cast out of human warmth, and asks Victor for one thing only, a companion made like himself. The terror here is not the stitched body on the table. It is the maker who gives a creature a mind and then refuses to answer for the loneliness he has made.

title: Pedro Páramo
author: Juan Rulfo
extract: I came to Comala because I had been told that my father, a man named Pedro Páramo, lived there.
blurb: The dead in Comala have not stopped talking. They murmur up through the floors and the broken walls of a town the heat hollowed out long ago, and into that quiet, which turns out to be no quiet at all, walks Juan Preciado, sent by his dying mother to find the father he never knew, a man named Pedro Páramo. She promised him a green paradise; he arrives to its ash. Pedro Páramo tells itself from inside death, fragments and ruptured time and voices you cannot sort into living or gone, until you give up trying. At the centre of every whisper is the cacique himself, whose power over Comala was absolute and who let the whole town wither when Susana San Juan, the one thing he ever truly wanted, drifted past his reach forever. Juan Rulfo wrote almost nothing else. He did not need to: here is the discovery that longing outlasts the body, and finds nowhere left to go.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Leo Tolstoy
extract: The previous history of Ivan Ilyitch was the simplest, the most ordinary, and the most awful.
blurb: Open the novella and Ivan Ilyich is already dead. His colleagues, reading the notice between cases, feel first the small private arithmetic of whose promotion now follows, then the relief that it is him and not them. This is the world Tolstoy lays bare: a respectable judge who furnished his life as carefully as his drawing room, every choice correct, tasteful, like everyone else's. Then a bruise in his side begins to ache, the ache will not stop, and it teaches him the one thing he arranged his whole existence never to learn. What torments him is not the pain but the lie kept up around his bed, the cheerful pretense that he is only ill and will surely recover. Only Gerasim, the peasant who holds his legs through the night, tells the truth by refusing to pretend. The most ordinary life, Tolstoy shows, can be the most terrible, and the question that breaks open in the dark, whether he lived as he ought to have, is one you will not put down once you have heard it asked.

title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
extract: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
blurb: It is much safer to be feared than loved: the sentence arrives without heat, without apology, the way a surgeon names the thing that has to be cut. That coolness is the whole unsettling genius of The Prince. For centuries the books written for rulers told them how to be good; Machiavelli, stripped of office and tortured by the Medici he would then dedicate it to, sat down to tell them instead how to survive, and the gap between those two instructions is the nerve he keeps pressing. A prince who insists on virtue among men who have none, he argues, will be destroyed, and cruelty used well and quickly is a kind of mercy. The examples come like evidence in a brief, Cesare Borgia, Moses, Romulus, never ornament. What lingers is not the shock of the conclusions but the calm, the sense of a man describing the world exactly as it is while everyone around him agrees to pretend otherwise. Read it once and you will hear its level voice under every speech a powerful man ever gave.

title: Four Quartets
author: T.S. Eliot
extract: The end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.
blurb: In the uncertain hour before the morning, after a night spent fire-watching over a burning London, Eliot meets a familiar compound ghost in the dead patrol of an emptied street, and the dead poet speaks to the living one. Four Quartets was built one poem at a time, the last three composed through the years of the war, each named for a place with a claim on him: an English manor garden, the Somerset village his ancestors left, a granite reef off the Massachusetts coast, a small Huntingdonshire chapel. The four circle one fixed idea, the still point of the turning world, where time and the timeless touch and an ordinary afternoon goes suddenly transparent. Read it aloud, as it asks to be read, and the verse moves like water finding its level, paradox folding into paradox, 'in my beginning is my end.' Eliot promises no easy comfort, only a discipline of attention so total that the fire which ends the poem both consumes and refines, until the fire and the rose are one.

title: Dover Beach
author: Matthew Arnold
extract: Ah, love, let us be true to one another!
blurb: Listen, the poem says, and the calm of the moonlit strait gives way to a sound: pebbles dragged down the shingle by the receding wave and flung up again, a grating roar that brings "the eternal note of sadness in." Matthew Arnold heard in that note what Sophocles heard long ago on the Aegean, and beneath it he hears the thing the whole poem is built to mourn: the Sea of Faith, once at the full and folded round the earth like a bright girdle, now drawing back down the vast edges of the world with a melancholy, long, withdrawing roar. With nothing left to guarantee the world's goodness, Arnold turns from the window to the one person beside him and makes the smallest, most human plea there is: ah, love, let us be true to one another. For the land of dreams before them has really neither joy, nor love, nor light, nor certitude, nor peace, nor help for pain, only a darkling plain swept by confused alarms, where ignorant armies clash by night.

title: The Man Without Qualities
author: Robert Musil
extract: If there is a sense of reality, there must also be a sense of possibility.
blurb: Vienna, 1913. A committee of the great and the good gathers to plan a jubilee for 1918, a festival of Austrian spirit meant to dazzle the whole of Europe; none of them can know the empire has barely two years left to exist. Into this hum of self-congratulation walks Ulrich, a gifted mathematician who has resolved to take a year's holiday from life itself, having earned every distinction a man could want and found that not one of them touches him. He is the man without qualities, not because he is empty but because he is too full: he holds what Musil calls the sense of possibility so completely that to settle on a single life would feel like quietly murdering all the others. The book thinks as it moves, breaking into essays mid-scene, endlessly deferring the moment when something must at last be decided. Musil gave it twenty years and died in Swiss exile with the final pages unwritten. A novel about a man who cannot commit could close no other way.

title: The Stranger
author: Albert Camus
extract: Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday; I can't be sure.
blurb: He buries his mother and does not cry. He smokes by her coffin, drinks coffee, and the next day goes to a comedy at the cinema and takes a lover. Weeks later, on a beach near Algiers, the sun pressing white against his eyes, Meursault fires a revolver into a man he barely knows, then four more times into a body already still, and can give no reason for it. The court that sentences Albert Camus's clerk to death is far less troubled by the killing than by the dry-eyed son at the graveside: society, The Stranger understands, will forgive almost any violence sooner than it will forgive a man who refuses to perform the grief expected of him. Camus writes in sentences scoured of all explanation, flat and sunstruck and strangely clean, the prose of a man who will not lie about what he feels even to save his own life. And the ending, when Meursault throws open his heart to the gentle indifference of the world, lands heavier than the gunshot.

title: The Bhagavad Gita
author: Vyasa
extract: Let right deeds be Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
blurb: Two armies stand drawn up for slaughter, conch shells ringing, and a warrior asks his charioteer to halt the horses in the empty ground between them. There Arjuna looks at the enemy and recognises his grandfather, his teachers, his cousins, and he cannot lift his bow. What follows is not a battle but a conversation: the charioteer is Krishna, god walking the earth as a friend, who refuses to let Arjuna's grief off easily. Across seven hundred Sanskrit verses he turns one man's failure of nerve into the largest questions there are: what dies when the body falls, how to act in a world you did not make, why work done without hunger for its reward is the only freedom. Then, asked for proof, Krishna grants Arjuna divine sight, and the soldier sees every world and every age blazing inside the god's countless mouths. The wonder of the Bhagavad Gita is that it holds the cosmos and a single trembling man in one breath, and tells you, without raising its voice, that you are standing on Arjuna's field already.

title: Fathers and Sons
author: Ivan Turgenev
extract: A nihilist is a man who does not bow down before any authority, who does not take any principle on faith.
blurb: Bow to no authority, take no principle on faith, accept nothing you cannot weigh or dissect: that is the creed Yevgeny Bazarov carries into his friend's family estate, frog specimens in hand, certain that love and art and aristocratic honour are so much sentimental rot. Turgenev gave this young man's faith its name, nihilism, and built him so completely that radicals and conservatives alike read the book and felt betrayed. The wonder of it is the tenderness. Turgenev loves Bazarov even as he dismantles him, and the instrument of the dismantling is Anna Odintsova, a widow whose unhurried composure strips the materialist of his own and leaves him in love against every conviction he owns, appalled by what he feels. Here is the recognition that aches: the certainty of the young, and the moment it cracks. Read it for the man undone by the single thing he swore was an illusion, the feeling he could not lay open on a table.

title: The Tin Drum
author: Günter Grass
extract: Even bad books are books and therefore sacred.
blurb: Listen for the drum. On his third birthday Oskar Matzerath decides the world of grown men is not worth growing into and throws himself down the cellar stairs, fixing his body at a child's height forever. From that knee-high vantage he watches Danzig go under: the flags climb the poles, the neighbours join the Party, the Jewish toyseller who supplied his drums is gone, and the only honest witness left is a boy too small to be blamed and too clear-eyed to look away. He carries two instruments, a tin drum that hammers the buried years back into the present and a scream pitched to shatter glass, every smug windowpane that would rather stay whole and silent. Günter Grass wrote the grotesque the way the century demanded, comedy and horror fused so close you cannot laugh without flinching. Narrating it all from a mental asylum, Oskar keeps the time the nation preferred to forget it ever kept.

title: All Quiet on the Western Front
author: Erich Maria Remarque
extract: This book is to be neither an accusation nor a confession, and least of all an adventure.
blurb: A pair of good leather boots passes from one dying boy to the next, each new owner inheriting them the moment the last is buried, a small grim economy that outlasts every man who laces them. This is the world Remarque hands you, the Western Front seen not by a general but by Paul Bäumer, a German schoolboy of nineteen who marched off because a teacher swore it was glorious, and who spends his short life learning what the teacher never had to. What sets this book apart from every other war story is its refusal to console. Paul lies trapped in a shell crater beside a French soldier he has just stabbed, finds in the dead man's pocket that he was a printer named Gérard Duval with a wife and child, and pleads forgiveness from a corpse. The enemy was a boy too. Remarque tells it in prose so flat and clear it leaves nowhere to look away, and the close is the cruelest stroke of all: the title is the lie the dispatches send home.

title: Buddenbrooks
author: Thomas Mann
extract: And -- and -- what comes next?
blurb: In the old gilt-edged book where the Buddenbrooks have recorded four generations of their births and deaths, little Hanno takes a pen and draws two clean lines beneath his own name. Asked why, he can only say he thought nothing more was coming. He is right. Thomas Mann's chronicle of a Lübeck grain dynasty is a study of how a family dies not from catastrophe but from refinement: each generation inherits the firm along with a finer, more trembling nervous system, until the commercial nerve thins entirely into music and longing and the wish to be left alone. Thomas the Senator reads Schopenhauer one winter night and tastes, for an hour, the dissolution of the self into something vast; by morning he is back at his desk, and it saves no one. The terrible tenderness of the book is that it loves what is killing them. To grow this beautiful, Mann saw, is to grow unfit to live.

title: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle
extract: Every art and every kind of inquiry, and likewise every act and purpose, seems to aim at some good.
blurb: You become a builder by building, Aristotle writes, and a lyre-player by playing the lyre; and so you become brave only by doing brave things, just only by doing just ones, until the doing has quietly made you into someone. This is the book's most consequential claim, and its most consoling too: virtue is not something you know but something you practise into being, laid down one ordinary choice at a time. The man who freezes in the crisis was not unlucky. Courage was simply never the habit. The Nicomachean Ethics takes up the oldest question there is, how a person ought to live, and answers it not with commandments but with the slow shaping of a character over a whole life. It gives two entire books to friendship, certain the good life cannot be lived alone, that you need another self in whom your own goodness becomes visible. Happiness, here, is never the reward for being good. It is what living well already is.

title: Speak Memory
author: Vladimir Nabokov
extract: Our existence is but a brief crack of light between two eternities of darkness.
blurb: On the veranda at Vyra there is a row of small coloured panes, and a boy presses his eye to each in turn, watching the same garden go ruby, then emerald, then a bruised yellow. Nabokov spends Speak, Memory doing exactly this: returning to a vanished Russian childhood and turning every detail until it surrenders its true colour. He was a serious lepidopterist, and he writes like one, pinning each governess, each summer, each butterfly net at the pond so that time cannot carry it off. The Russia he recovers had already been destroyed by the time he wrote, which is why the precision aches: it is salvage work, conducted from memory's last specimens. But remembrance is only half of it. Nabokov is hunting the hidden rhymes of a life, images that return across the decades like a fate disclosing itself, and he finds them. Memory, the book argues, does not merely keep the past. Pressed hard enough, it reveals a design no one alive ever planned.

title: The Consolation of Philosophy
author: Boethius
day: International Day of the Imprisoned Writer
extract: nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so
blurb: In a prison cell at Pavia, a condemned man is weeping over his ruin when a woman appears at his side and tells him to stop. It is Philosophy herself, come to reason him out of his grief. Boethius had been consul, the most powerful civilian in Italy, until a charge of treason under Theodoric left him awaiting execution. What he wrote in those last months is neither plea nor prayer but a conversation, alternating prose and verse, in which Fortune's wheel turns exactly as it must, raising and dropping every life without malice, because nothing it lends was ever truly given. Wealth, office, reputation: loans, all of them, and all recalled. Only the reasoning soul holds anything that cannot be seized. For a thousand years the grieving reached for this book, Alfred and Chaucer and Elizabeth I among those who translated it, and found a man at the edge of death still insisting, gently, that the argument held.

title: Blindness
author: José Saramago
extract: If you can see, look. If you can look, observe.
blurb: The blindness, when it comes, is not darkness but a luminous white, a sea of milk that floods the eyes of one driver stopped at a traffic light and then, person by person, an entire city. The state does what states do and locks the infected away in a derelict asylum, then forgets to feed them. Among the quarantined is one woman who can still see, the doctor's wife, who faked the disease to follow her husband inside and now alone must watch what everyone else is spared. Saramago gives no one a name, only their afflictions and their roles, so the crowd becomes every crowd. His sentences run on for half a page, commas stitching speaker to speaker without a single quotation mark, the grammar itself going gradually sightless. What she witnesses as the wards turn to filth and predation is unbearable, and the novel's terrible wager is that sight, here, is the curse and the conscience both.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
author: J.D. Salinger
extract: A book that, when you're all done reading it, you wish the author that wrote it was a terrific friend of yours.
blurb: Where do the ducks in the Central Park lagoon go when the water freezes over? Holden Caulfield keeps asking it, of cab drivers, of the night, of anyone who'll listen, and the question gives him away: under all the scorn is a sixteen-year-old frightened of what becomes of small things when the cold comes. Newly expelled from his fourth school, he spends three December days wandering New York rather than going home, and the whole book is his voice talking to you, funny and aggrieved and able to spot a phony across a room while missing the one he's becoming. The grief he won't name is his dead brother Allie, whose baseball mitt was covered in poems in green ink. He dreams of standing at the edge of a cliff in a field of rye, catching children before they fall into whatever ruined him. You finish it wishing he were a friend you could call.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
extract: Nolite te bastardes carborundorum.
blurb: Scratched into the floor of a closet, in a hand its new occupant will never match to a face, is a line of schoolroom Latin a woman left there before her: nolite te bastardes carborundorum, don't let the bastards grind you down. The closet belongs to a Commander in the Republic of Gilead, and the woman who finds it is called Offred because she now belongs to a man named Fred, forbidden to hold money, forbidden even to read the words she has just discovered. Margaret Atwood built Gilead out of the historical record and invented none of its cruelties, and that is the source of its particular dread: you cannot find the moment where this becomes impossible, only the moments where it became convenient. Offred hoards memory the way the starving hoard bread, her stolen name, her daughter's weight in her arms, her husband's face going soft at the edges. Read it once and you will never again trust that the ground beneath an ordinary life is solid.

title: The Republic
author: Plato
extract: Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy
blurb: Imagine a ring that makes you invisible. Glaucon sets it on the table early and asks the only question that matters: stripped of every reward, with no chance of being caught, would you still choose to be just, or is decency merely the price we pay for fear? Socrates refuses the easy answer and instead builds an entire city in speech, hoping to find justice written large enough to read, mapping the soul's three voices (reason, spirit, appetite) onto three classes until justice reveals itself as a kind of inner health and injustice a sickness its sufferer cannot feel. At the book's heart waits the Allegory of the Cave, where prisoners chained since birth take shadows on a wall for the whole world, and the one who escapes finds the climb toward the sun so blinding the others would kill him before they would follow. By the end, the tyrant who seems to have seized everything carries the most ruined soul in the city. A quarrel about fairness has become the first true map of the human interior.

title: White Noise
author: Don DeLillo
extract: The station wagons arrived at noon, a long shining line that coursed through the west campus.
blurb: In White Noise the brand names surface like incantations, Toyota Celica murmured by a sleeping child, the litany of products intoned over the supermarket aisles as if the packaging might answer the question nobody in this Ohio town will say aloud. Don DeLillo gives us Jack Gladney, who founded the field of Hitler Studies and cannot read German, his wife Babette, and a household so funny and tender you almost forget what the comedy is built to hold off. Then a train derails, a black chemical cloud blooms over the town, and the airborne toxic event drags the joke into the open: everyone here is terrified of dying, Babette so totally she has traded her body for a pill engineered to delete the fear, and the pill does not work. What DeLillo hears, under the hum of catalogs and televised weather, is a whole country refusing to think the one thought it cannot stop thinking. The most photographed barn in America stands right there on the highway, and no one can see it anymore, only the photographing of it.

title: Dead Souls
author: Nikolai Gogol
extract: Russia, whither flyest thou? Answer! She gives no answer.
blurb: Picture a polite, well-fed stranger seated across the table from a country landowner, naming a price for the serfs who have died since the last census but linger on the tax rolls as though they still breathed. That is Chichikov's scheme, and the provinces oblige him: estate by estate he gathers the dead, and estate by estate Gogol uncovers the living, from the sugary dreamer Manilov to old Plyushkin, a miser who has hoarded himself down to something barely human. The comedy is merciless, and the sorrow beneath it never fully lifts, because the joke keeps turning out to be true. Gogol conceived the book as the inferno of a Dantean epic; in a crisis of conscience he burned the road toward paradise, and died before he could write it again. What remains is the laughter and the long open road, and that startling moment near the end when the whole country becomes a hurtling troika: Russia, whither flyest thou? She gives no answer, and the silence is the entire book.

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
extract: The growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts.
blurb: Edward Casaubon has poured his life into a book called the Key to All Mythologies, a great work he will never finish, and Dorothea Brooke, ardent and not yet twenty, marries him certain she can help him carry it. That mismatch is where Middlemarch begins, before George Eliot widens the lens to hold a whole Midlands town: the gifted young doctor Lydgate, whose reforming ideals wear away under debt and his wife's lovely, immovable will; the banker Bulstrode, whose piety papers over an old crime; Fred Vincy, waiting slowly to deserve Mary Garth. Eliot knows every one of them from the inside, with a sympathy so exact it can name the very hour an idealism begins to shrink. She wrote that if we truly felt all ordinary human life we would hear the grass grow and the squirrel's heart beat, and die of the roar that lies on the other side of silence. No other novel takes you so close to that roar, or sends you back into your own small life so much gentler for having heard it.

title: Death Fugue
author: Paul Celan
extract: Black milk of daybreak we drink it at evening we drink it at midday and morning we drink it at night.
blurb: In a death camp, prisoners are ordered to play dance music while others shovel a grave in the air, and from that obscenity Paul Celan built a poem that refuses to console. Its refrain, black milk of daybreak, is drunk at morning and noon and evening and night, the impossible phrase wheeling back the way a subject wheels through a fugue, gathering a weight it should not be able to carry. A commandant writes home to Germany, calls golden-haired Margarete to mind, plays with his serpents, and orders the prisoners to play death more sweetly, for death is a master from Deutschland. Celan, whose mother was shot and whose father died in the camps, refused both the false comfort of testimony and the lie of silence. By the close, Margarete's golden hair set against Shulamith's hair of ash, Death Fugue will not let you stand apart from the dead.

title: Tristram Shandy
author: Laurence Sterne
extract: I wish either my father or my mother, or indeed both of them, had minded what they were about when they begot me.
blurb: The book begins at the exact moment of its hero's conception, and immediately derails: mid-act, Mrs Shandy asks whether her husband has remembered to wind the clock, and Tristram blames every misfortune of his life on the interruption. That is the engine of the whole thing. Tristram sets out to write his life and cannot get near it, because telling any one minute breeds three more minutes worth telling, and because nobody in the house will stop talking. Nine volumes pass; he is barely born. What looks like chaos is the tenderest argument about people ever smuggled into a joke. Uncle Toby, gentle and wounded, lives forever inside the siege that maimed him, rebuilding it in miniature on the bowling green; Walter spins theories about noses and Christian names that no fact will ever confirm. Laurence Sterne gives you a blank page, a black page, a marbled page, and a hand-drawn squiggle for a plot, and somehow it is the most loving book in English about how hopelessly we each live trapped inside our own heads.

author: Roberto Bolaño
day: International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women
extract: Reading is like thinking, like praying, like talking to a friend, like expressing your ideas, like listening to other people's ideas.
blurb: In a Mexican border city the bodies of women keep turning up, in vacant lots, in the desert, behind a school, and the files pile up unsolved. Roberto Bolaño's enormous posthumous novel circles that fact in five movements and never lets you forget it is there. Four European scholars chase a vanished German novelist across continents; a philosophy professor comes apart in the desert heat; an American reporter flies in to cover a boxing match and feels a wrongness he cannot name. Then arrives the part about the crimes, nearly three hundred pages in the flat, exhausted language of a coroner's report, one murdered woman after another, until the catalogue becomes the most damning thing fiction has dared to attempt. Bolaño wrote it knowing he was dying, and the book refuses every consolation a smaller one would reach for. It cannot redeem what it shows you. It only asks, with terrible patience, that you do not look away.

title: Gilead
author: Marilynne Robinson
extract: I told you last night that I might be gone sometime, and you said, Where, and I said, To be with the Good Lord.
blurb: Water comes down off a shaken branch onto a young couple laughing in the rain, and the old minister on his porch decides that water must have been made first for blessing and only afterward for crops and the wash. John Ames is seventy-six, his heart failing, and his son is seven, too small to remember him, so Ames sits down to write the boy a letter to be opened once he is grown, and the letter becomes this book. Gilead is Robinson's argument, made in prose so quiet you find yourself holding your breath, that the ordinary world looked at hard enough is indistinguishable from grace: light moving on the river, the smell of a baseball mitt, the face of the young wife who came to him late. Ames cannot hold to a thought without turning aside to bless whatever has caught his eye, and that turning aside is the entire faith of the book. To read it is to be taught, sentence by sentence, how much of your own life you have failed to notice.

title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
extract: In the department of - but it is better not to mention the department.
blurb: Akaky Akakievich loves the alphabet. A copying clerk in a St. Petersburg department too dull to name, he has no ambition beyond a clean transcription, certain letters his favourites, and the work brings him a private rapture that needs nothing else. Then a tailor tells him his coat is past mending, and the saving begins: months without supper, without candlelight, the future narrowed to one garment he can almost feel on his shoulders. When the coat finally comes it is the happiest day of his life, and Gogol's narrator, who has been mocking this little man for pages, suddenly cannot keep it up. There is a moment when a young clerk's joke falters and he hears, underneath it, I am your brother. That is the whole revolution of the story. The coat is stolen, the city that never noticed Akaky shrugs, and out of his death something walks back through the snow to collect what it is owed. Russian literature's tenderness for the overlooked begins here, improbably, in laughter.

title: Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
extract: Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.
blurb: For ten years a watchman has lain on the roof of Argos, waiting for the fire that means Troy has fallen and the king sails home. When the beacon finally leaps across the hills, it lights the way to a murder: Clytemnestra has drawn her husband a bath and laid out a robe stitched shut, and she has waited longer than he has. So begins the only Greek trilogy to reach us whole, three plays that set a killing in the first, its answering killing in the second, and on the third the question beneath both. What happens when every act of justice is also a crime, when blood can only call for more blood? Orestes avenges his father by killing his mother, and the Furies, older than the gods and deaf to his reasons, hunt him down. The wonder of the Oresteia is that it refuses to end in more blood. It ends in a courtroom, the first one, the law invented in front of you because the only other road is a house that never stops bleeding.

title: Long Day's Journey into Night
author: Eugene O'Neill
extract: None of us can help the things life has done to us.
blurb: By nightfall a foghorn is moaning out on the Sound, and inside the summer house the four Tyrones have talked their way back through every betrayal they have ever handed one another. Mary drifts upstairs and returns changed, the morphine pulling her out of reach while her husband and sons pretend not to see; James, the matinee idol who traded his talent for a sure thing, counts the cost of every lamp left burning; Jamie drinks; Edmund, the youngest, coughs and waits to hear how bad his lungs really are. Eugene O'Neill set down his own family here, sealed the manuscript, and asked that it never be staged in his lifetime. What binds these four is not cruelty but love so wounded it can only come out as blame. The fog they each long for is the time before the harm was done, and the night the title keeps promising is what is left when even that fog will not hold.

title: Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain
extract: All right, then, I'll go to hell.
blurb: Two days downriver and the raft has slipped past Cairo in the fog, which means it is carrying Huck and Jim deeper into slave country instead of out of it, and Huck still cannot decide whether to turn his friend in. The wonder of the book is the voice: a barefoot, half-schooled boy telling his own story in the river dialect of the antebellum South, funny and sharp and wholly unable to see that he is the only decent soul in the frame. Twain crowds the banks with America at its worst, two grifters working the river towns, genteel families shooting each other over nothing, a father drunk and dangerous, until cruelty reads as the ordinary weather of the place. So when Huck resolves to help Jim run, he is certain he is damning himself, and you watch a boy do the bravest thing in American literature while believing it the worst. Few novels have made goodness this funny, or this costly to the one who carries it.

title: Notes of a Native Son
author: James Baldwin
extract: On the 29th of July, in 1943, my father died. On the same day, a few hours later, his last child was born.
blurb: On the morning his father was buried, Baldwin rode to the graveyard through streets carpeted with the smashed plate glass of the Harlem riot. His father had died the day the family's youngest child was born, and the funeral fell on Baldwin's nineteenth birthday, so that private mourning and a city on fire collided in one unbearable week. Out of that coincidence he builds his greatest essay: a portrait of a proud, paranoid, bitter preacher of a father, and the slow terror of discovering that the very bitterness that helped kill the man had taken root in the son. Watch him hurl a water glass at a New Jersey waitress who will not serve him, and feel the rage he says no Black American is without, a fever to be lived with or surrendered to. The prose moves with the cadence of the pulpit he was raised in. It closes by handing you two commandments you must somehow keep at once, and you carry them out of the book.

title: Prometheus Unbound
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
day: International Day for the Abolition of Slavery
extract: To suffer woes which Hope thinks infinite; To forgive wrongs darker than death or night;
blurb: Three thousand years chained to a crag in the Caucasus, his flesh torn each dawn, the Titan who stole fire for mankind has every reason to want his tyrant dead. Instead, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound opens with Prometheus recalling the curse he once hurled at Jupiter, wishing now that no living thing should suffer as he has. That single act of withdrawn hatred is the revolution: Jupiter falls not to an army but to the moment his victim refuses to mirror him, and the shapeless power beneath all things, Demogorgon, rises to sweep him into the abyss. What Aeschylus resolved by reconciliation, Shelley remakes into something stranger and braver, a universe transfigured from the inside out, beginning with one spirit's change of heart. The verse is dense, exalted, almost unsingable in its reach, yet Asia's "My soul is an enchanted boat" floats free as pure music. To forgive wrongs darker than death or night, the poem insists, is the only freedom worth the name.

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Joseph Conrad
extract: The horror! The horror!
blurb: Dusk gathers on the Thames, and as the great waterway to the ends of the earth goes still, a man named Marlow says the strangest thing: this too has been one of the dark places of the earth. Then he tells how he piloted a battered steamboat up the Congo to fetch a legendary ivory agent named Kurtz, and how every mile of river turned the journey inward. Conrad writes the approach as a slow drowning of certainty. The prose grows foggy and hypnotic, the sentences losing their footing as Marlow advances, until what waits upriver is not a man but a hollow where one used to stand. Kurtz has crossed the line civilisation swore it would never cross, and let himself be worshipped as a god to do it. The book will not let you watch from a safe distance; it implicates the calm London evening, and you in it. So when his last words come, the horror, the horror, hear them not as a verdict on the jungle but as one on us.

title: Notes on "Camp"
author: Susan Sontag
extract: The whole point of Camp is to dethrone the serious.
blurb: Fifty-eight numbered jottings, dedicated to the memory of Oscar Wilde, and by the last one you cannot unsee the thing they name. Susan Sontag set out to describe a sensibility no one had pinned down, the taste that adores a Tiffany lamp, a feather boa, an old movie too gorgeous to be any good, precisely because each is too much. Camp, she writes, is a love of the unnatural, of artifice and exaggeration, a way of seeing the whole world in quotation marks. The thrill is that the essay never flattens its subject into an argument. It performs it instead, aphoristic and sly, half in love with the extravagance it dissects, serious about the frivolous and frivolous about the serious. Read it once and you start noticing camp everywhere, in a friend's ironic devotion, in a diva's grand terrible gesture. The ultimate camp statement, she decides, is that a thing can be good because it is awful.

title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
author: Joan Didion
extract: The center was not holding.
blurb: San Francisco, the cold spring of 1967, and the missing children of America were gathering in the Haight to call themselves hippies. Joan Didion went to find them and came back with the coldest, clearest report anyone filed on a generation coming loose from its moorings. She borrowed her title from Yeats, from the rough beast slouching toward Bethlehem, because that was the atmosphere she felt in the panhandle: not a revolution, not a siege, but a center that was not holding, a society that had forgotten to teach its youngest the rules of its own game. What makes the essay unbearable is her refusal to editorialize. She simply watches, records the flat sad talk of runaways and drifters and the smallest children, and lets the detail do the indicting. Read it once and you will never again mistake the Summer of Love for a party, or forget the youngest faces she found at the end of it.

title: Clarissa
author: Samuel Richardson
extract: A feeling heart is a blessing that no one, who has it, would be without.
blurb: Two people sit writing letters about the same events, and the horror is that you believe them both. Lovelace is the most charming correspondent in English fiction, witty, quicksilver, confessing his schemes with such relish that you almost root for him even as he closes a trap around a girl of eighteen. Clarissa Harlowe writes from inside it: hounded by a family who would sell her to a man she cannot bear, then manoeuvred toward a rake who has decided her virtue is a fortress worth the siege. Across nearly a million words, Samuel Richardson lets you watch the slow machinery of ruin grind, letter answering letter, and makes you feel how a world that calls a woman good only when she submits has already done the seducer's work for him. What undoes you is her clarity. She sees the danger, reasons against it, and the trap shuts anyway.

title: Song of Solomon
author: Toni Morrison
extract: You wanna fly, you got to give up the shit that weighs you down.
blurb: In a dusty Virginia town, children clasp hands and circle and sing a rhyme nobody can explain, a song about a man named Solomon who rose into the air and flew, and Milkman Dead, who came south chasing a rumor of gold, slowly understands that the nonsense is the only surviving record of his own great-grandfather. Song of Solomon takes hold of the African American legend of the Flying Africans, the enslaved who, the story goes, simply rose from the fields and went home across the water, and asks the question the legend buries: Solomon flew to freedom and left twenty-one children earthbound behind him. Morrison weighs names like gold here. Dead was a drunk soldier's slip of the pen in a Freedmen's ledger; Pilate carries hers in a brass box at her ear because her father, who could not read, copied the shape from the Bible. The book ends at the lip of a leap, where surrender to the air is freedom and abandonment in one motion, the old choice made again.

title: The Dhammapada
author: Anonymous
extract: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
blurb: Hatred is never appeased by hatred; by love alone is it appeased. The Buddha is said to have spoken that line, and the centuries between have not dulled it. The Dhammapada gathers 423 such verses, the most beloved distillation of his teaching, and it asks you to believe nothing. There are no miracles here, no god to petition, no reward dangled past death. There is only a claim, stated in the opening line and proved across every chapter that follows: the mind makes everything, your joy and your suffering both, and so the work of becoming free is work no one can do for you. What unsettles is how gently it says this. The verses on desire and anger, on the sage who has crossed the flood, were shaped to be memorized, and they behave like seeds, dry and complete, apt to open hours after you have shut the book. To read it is to be handed full responsibility for your own mind, and to feel, against all expectation, lighter for the weight.

title: Paradise Lost
author: John Milton
extract: Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.
blurb: Hurled flaming out of Heaven, Satan lifts his head from a lake of fire and, surveying the ruin of everything he was, decides he would rather rule this pit than kneel in paradise. Milton gives the Devil the grandest voice in the language, and the terrible thrill of the poem is how much you feel his defiance before you learn to distrust it. From that burning floor the poem opens outward to hold the whole cosmos at once: the war in Heaven, the void of Chaos, the making of the world, and two naked people in a garden who have been told not to eat one thing. It is written in blank verse that rolls like an organ, clause piling on clause until a single sentence carries the weight of a falling empire. Milton set out to justify the ways of God to men, and wrote instead the most magnificent account of loss we have: the morning two people walk out of Eden, hand in hand, into the world that is ours.

title: Because I could not stop for Death
author: Emily Dickinson
extract: Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me;
blurb: Death comes as a suitor. He pulls up in a carriage, unhurried, perfectly mannered, and because the speaker has no time to spare he makes the time for her, handing her in beside a silent third passenger named Immortality. What follows is the strangest courtship in American poetry: a slow drive past children circling a schoolyard, past fields of grain that seem to gaze back, past a sun that does not set so much as pass them, until the horses pause before a house that is only a swelling of the ground. Dickinson set all of this to the meter of the hymns she sang as a girl, so the lines rock with the cadence of Sunday worship even as they decline its comfort. She let almost none of her poems out into the world while she lived. This one waited in a drawer to tell you, centuries on, that eternity feels shorter than a single afternoon.

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
extract: I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed. What have ye done to surpass man?
blurb: In a forest at the edge of the world, Zarathustra meets an old hermit still singing his devotions to God, and walks on astonished that the saint has not yet heard the news the book will carry down into the marketplace: that God is dead, and the work of becoming human has only now begun. Nietzsche wrote his hardest thinking not as argument but as scripture, in parables and songs and a voice that swings between ecstasy and laughter, certain that logic would only tame what he had to say. He teaches the Overman, man as a rope stretched over an abyss, something to be surpassed rather than worshipped. And he sets down the heaviest question philosophy has ever asked: could you love your one life so completely that you would will every moment of it back, unchanged, forever. The book does not persuade so much as press, and what it presses for is a different way of carrying your days. Zarathustra ends alone, walking out glowing into his morning, having kept no last disciple.

title: Madame Bovary
author: Gustave Flaubert
extract: Human speech is like a cracked tin kettle, on which we hammer out tunes to make bears dance when we long to move the stars.
blurb: At the county agricultural fair, a man leans close to Emma Bovary and murmurs about two souls drawn together by fate, while a voice from the platform below awards medals for manure and the fattest sow. Flaubert runs the two together in a single passage, the seducer's borrowed romance and the bellowing over prize livestock, and that cruel counterpoint is the whole book in miniature. Emma wants a life as large as the convent novels that ruined her, and she has been handed provincial Normandy instead: a kind, dull husband who smells of the surgery, lovers who desire her without ever once seeing her. What changed fiction forever is how close Flaubert stands to her, slipping inside her longing so completely that you cannot tell scorn from pity, cannot keep your own hunger for something finer apart from hers. The French took her name for the sickness of wanting to be someone you are not, and the novel earns it by making that wanting feel, from inside a life this small, like the only sane thing left.

title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
extract: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
blurb: Seven sentences hold up the entire book, the first six branching downward into decimals like a logical tree, the seventh standing alone: whatever we cannot speak about, we must pass over in silence. Ludwig Wittgenstein worked out this architecture in notebooks he carried as a soldier through the First World War, finishing it as a prisoner of war, certain he had dissolved every genuine problem philosophy had ever posed. The pages build a theory of how a sentence pictures the world, fact answering to fact, and then press toward the border of what language can reach at all. Ethics, beauty, the meaning of a life: all of it, he insists, lives on the far side of that border, where nothing can be said and everything that matters is merely shown. Then each proposition, he tells you, is revealed as a rung; understand them and you throw the ladder away and see the world rightly. Few books ask to be climbed only to be abandoned, or make that abandonment feel like the only honest place to stand.

title: The Lottery
author: Shirley Jackson
extract: It isn't fair, it isn't right, Mrs. Hutchinson screamed, and then they were upon her.
blurb: The children come first, on a clear June morning, filling their pockets with the smoothest stones and building the rest into a tidy pile while the grown-ups drift into the square and talk of planting and rain, tractors and taxes. Shirley Jackson lets the morning stay ordinary for a long time, so ordinary you forget to be afraid, which is exactly the trap. When The New Yorker ran the story, readers cancelled their subscriptions in fury and wrote to demand where this village was, as if it could be anywhere but the town they already lived in. That is the thing Jackson knew and proved in ten unhurried pages: that the worst things people do are not done in rage but in routine, with a black box and a slip of paper and a date that comes round every year. The horror is not that the village holds a lottery. It is that no one can remember why, and no one thinks to stop.

title: The Temple of the Golden Pavilion
author: Yukio Mishima
extract: Ever since my childhood, Father had often spoken to me about the Golden Temple.
blurb: Picture the Golden Pavilion on its still pond in Kyoto, doubled in the water, gold against the dark trees, so finished and so perfect that it leaves no room for the boy looking at it. Mizoguchi is that boy: a novice monk, ugly, friendless, his stutter a permanent wall between himself and the moment he is trying to live. Mishima drew him from the acolyte who really did burn the temple to the ground in 1950, and he uses that fact to ask something genuinely frightening. What if beauty at its highest does not console you but shuts you out, arriving in the mind at the exact instant you reach for an ordinary life and cancelling it? The voice that carries this is slow, scrupulous, almost loving toward its own ruin, a mind refined past the point of living. By the time the flames come, you understand them, and that is the unbearable part.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
extract: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
blurb: At a country assembly, Mr. Darcy looks at Elizabeth Bennet across the room and pronounces her tolerable, but not handsome enough to tempt me, and she, overhearing, laughs and repeats it to her friends. From that small slight grows the most satisfying misjudgement in English fiction. Elizabeth is quick, certain, and delicious company, and she decides within an evening that she has Darcy entirely measured; Austen writes her so far inside free indirect discourse that the reader sits within that certainty and feels it shatter at the very moment she does. The book is really about the distance between being clever and being right, and the private mortification of discovering, too late, that you took the first for the second. That cost arrives as comedy, as blush, as something close to rescue: when these two finally see each other plainly, the relief is almost physical. Few novels make you ache this hard for two people to stop being fools and admit they are in love.

title: The Good Soldier
author: Ford Madox Ford
extract: This is the saddest story I have ever heard.
blurb: "This is the saddest story I have ever heard." So John Dowell begins, and the strangeness takes a moment to land: he was there for all of it, the sadness is largely his own, and he is the one person who still cannot see it. Across nine years of taking the waters at a German spa, two couples keep a flawless picture of Edwardian decency while Florence Dowell carries on an affair with Edward Ashburnham, the good soldier of the title, a man whose honour answers to every code the world can see and none that it cannot. Leonora, Edward's wife, has known the whole time. Dowell, telling it backward from the rubble of all four lives, will not quite let himself know even now. To read him is to feel his most soothing sentences as the ones burying the most, and to do the work he refuses, assembling from each calm digression a ruin that was always in plain sight. The saddest story is the one he cannot bear to finish hearing.

title: One Thousand and One Nights
author: Anonymous
extract: And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say.
blurb: Dawn is a death sentence. The king has buried a wife every morning for three years, and tonight the turn is Scheherazade's, except she has begun a story she will not finish before the light comes, and a king who must know how it ends cannot kill the only mouth that can tell him. One Thousand and One Nights is the great proof that narrative is not ornament but survival: every tale she spins, of Sinbad swallowed by whirlpools, of djinn loosed from sealed brass, of caliphs prowling Baghdad in disguise to glimpse the lives their palaces hide, is also an argument made beneath the sword that a story can purchase one more sunrise. The pleasure is bottomless, a door opening onto a door opening onto a door. What you carry away is not a book but a discovery: that to be listened to is to be spared, and that the right tale, told well, can hold a blade in the air.

title: The Sickness Unto Death
author: Søren Kierkegaard
extract: The self is a relation that relates itself to itself.
blurb: You can be busy, well-liked, untroubled, and entirely lost to yourself, and this is the book that will tell you so. Writing as Anti-Climacus, a height of Christian faith he openly placed above his own, Kierkegaard recasts despair as something far stranger than sadness: a quiet misrelation in which the self refuses to become the self it was made to be, refuses to rest in the power that grounds it. He builds the argument as a taxonomy, three forms of despair across three shapes of selfhood, and the unbearable thing is how precisely each one finds you. The despair that does not know it is despair, he insists, is not the gentlest but the deadliest; to feel completely at home in the world is already to have misplaced your soul. And the sickness named in the title cannot do the one thing sickness does. It will not kill. It only keeps you dying, awake to a wound you have spent a lifetime calling contentment.

title: Persuasion
author: Jane Austen
extract: You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope.
blurb: Eight years ago Anne Elliot let herself be talked out of the only love she would ever feel, and she has been quietly paying for it ever since. She is twenty-seven now, her bloom faded, treated as furniture by a vain father and a colder sister, when Frederick Wentworth, the naval officer she once refused, comes back rich and admired and seemingly indifferent to her. Persuasion is Austen's last finished novel and her most autumnal, the one where the wit cools into something close to grief: its heroine is not too clever for her own good but too constant, and the book lives inside her steady, unregarded mind while everyone around her mistakes her for no one. Austen wrote it knowing she was ill, and the ache of a second spring, of bloom recovered late, runs all through it. When Wentworth finally sets down his pen and lets Anne read what he could never say aloud, the irony falls away completely, and so does the reader's composure.

title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
author: Robert Frost
extract: The woods are lovely, dark and deep, but I have promises to keep, and miles to go before I sleep.
blurb: Snow is falling, and a man has reined in his horse on the darkest evening of the year, before woods that belong to someone back in the village, someone who will never know he stopped here to watch them fill. That is the whole event: a halt, a hush, no errand and no reason, only the pull of something lovely, dark and deep that asks for nothing and offers, in the same breath, rest and the kind of rest there is no waking from. Frost lets the rhyme do the seducing, each stanza handing its odd line forward into the next like a held breath, the snow and the meter coming down at the same pace. Then the turn, said twice: promises to keep, and miles to go before I sleep. He speaks it once as plain fact and once as a man talking himself back onto the road, and under that second saying you can hear how much of him wanted to stay in the snow.

title: Phèdre
author: Jean Racine
extract: No longer is it love hid in my heart, but Venus in her might seizing her prey.
blurb: She is the granddaughter of the sun, and she cannot bear the light. Phèdre has hidden her love for Hippolytus, her husband's son, until the rumor of Theseus's death loosens her tongue and the confession pours out, fully formed, with nowhere left to go. Then Theseus walks back through the door alive. Jean Racine wrote her ruin in alexandrines so taut they seem to hold their breath, twelve syllables tightening like a noose around a woman who knows an innocent man will die for her and cannot make herself speak the one word that would save him. The genius is in the splitting of her guilt: Venus seeded the desire in her blood before the play began, so the wanting is not her crime, but the silence is, and the silence is what kills. Few tragedies burn this slowly or this clean. Watch her walk into the dark with her eyes wide open, and you will understand why the French call this the most perfect thing their language has made.

title: The Leopard
author: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
extract: If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.
blurb: Don Fabrizio, Prince of Salina, climbs to his observatory at night because the stars are the only things in Sicily that will not betray him by changing. Below, in 1860, Garibaldi's redshirts are landing, and the feudal world his family has ruled for centuries is quietly ending. His clever nephew Tancredi offers the formula that will let the aristocracy survive by surrendering: for everything to stay the same, everything must change. Lampedusa, the last prince of his own dying line, wrote this while himself near death, and that doubling gives the book its terrible authority. Fabrizio is not fooled. He knows the new world that absorbs his class is genuinely smaller, coarser, less beautiful, and he watches it arrive with a grief too lucid for nostalgia. Read it for the prose that moves like a Sicilian afternoon, slow and golden and already mourning the light it is losing.

title: The Book of Job
author: Anonymous
extract: The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
blurb: Heaven makes a bet. God lets an accuser strip a blameless man of his children, his wealth, and his health, to see whether he will curse God for it, and what follows is the oldest unflinching cry against undeserved suffering ever set down. Job's three friends come to console him and stay to accuse: surely he sinned, surely the world is just and he has earned his ruin. Job will not say it. He sits in the ash and demands an answer from the silence, and the silence holds, chapter after chapter, until God speaks at last from a whirlwind. What comes is not an explanation but a question, vast and unbearably beautiful: where were you when the morning stars sang together, when the foundations of the earth were laid? The whirlwind does not solve the problem of pain; it dwarfs it. And the book, astonishingly, takes the side of the man who refused every easy comfort and demanded the truth instead.

title: A Christmas Carol
author: Charles Dickens
extract: Marley was dead: to begin with.
blurb: Marley was dead, to begin with. His partner seven years in the grave, Ebenezer Scrooge spends his evenings alone in a cold counting house, treating kindness as waste and pleasure as debt, until the dead man's chain comes dragging up the stair. Dickens built it as a ghost story, but the terror runs backward. The three spirits who come for Scrooge do not threaten him with hell. They walk him back through his own life: the boy left alone at school, reading by a low fire while the other children went home for Christmas; the young woman who loved him and watched him choose the ledger over her. Scene by scene the cruelty is given a source and a cost, until the last and most fearful spirit shows him a neglected grave with his own name cut into the stone. That is why Scrooge waking on Christmas morning, breathless and laughing and good, is among the most joyful figures in fiction. The warmth is no trick of the season. It was earned out of everything that first went cold.

title: Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard
author: Thomas Gray
extract: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day, the lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea.
blurb: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day; a plowman trudges home, the light leaves the fields, and one man is left among the slanting headstones of a country churchyard as the dark comes on. What Thomas Gray does here had scarcely been done before. He turns the full ceremonial weight of elegy, the grand form built for the great and the mourned, upon the people beneath the rudest stones, the farm laborers no chronicle will ever name. He wonders what they might have been: some mute inglorious Milton, some village Hampden who once faced down a petty local tyrant, and he asks whether a life lived unknown is a loss or a mercy, a sparing from the world's worst temptations. Then comes the quiet miracle. The poem turns, and the man grieving strangers begins, without quite saying so, to grieve himself, to picture the hour some kindred spirit reads his own stone. Few poems have made such tenderness out of the fear of being forgotten.

title: Infinite Jest
author: David Foster Wallace
extract: I am seated in an office, surrounded by heads and bodies.
blurb: Somewhere there is a film so perfectly entertaining that anyone who watches it cannot stop, forgets to eat or sleep or move, and dies in front of the screen, content. Three worlds revolve around that lethal cartridge in David Foster Wallace's Infinite Jest: a tennis academy full of gifted, joyless teenagers; a Boston halfway house where addicts crawl through early recovery one unglamorous day at a time; and a cell of wheelchair-bound Québécois separatists hunting the film as a weapon. The book runs a thousand pages and carries 388 endnotes, and the endnotes are not a stunt; they are the disease itself made into form, a mind so busy footnoting its own experience that it cannot simply live it. What the novel wants, underneath all the dazzle, is almost unbearably simple: to feel something real in a culture engineered to amuse you to death. Don Gately, a huge and gentle man clawing his way through early sobriety, carries that wish further than anyone, and he will break your heart trying.

title: The Idiot
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
extract: Beauty will save the world.
blurb: There is a moment, in the seconds before a seizure takes him, when Prince Myshkin feels every jarring thing in existence fall into one harmony so perfect he would give his whole life for it. He arrives in Petersburg from a Swiss clinic carrying no cunning and no self-defense, only a clarity so total that the people around him read it as idiocy. Dostoevsky set himself the hardest task in all of fiction, to put a genuinely good man on the page, and his discovery was stranger than failure: goodness like this is not beaten by the world's cruelty but by what it does to those who need it most. To love the ruined Nastasya Filippovna is to insist she is worth saving, and that is the one tenderness she cannot bear. The novel moves at a fever, scenes erupting in drawing rooms and on railway platforms, confessions blurted to strangers, every evening ending in some fresh public wound. Beauty will save the world, Myshkin believes, and the book spends six hundred pages testing whether the world will let it.

title: The Canterbury Tales
author: Geoffrey Chaucer
extract: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote, the droghte of March hath perced to the roote.
blurb: Say the first line aloud and something startling happens. "Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote" is six hundred years old, yet you can almost hear yourself inside it, English being born on the tongue. Geoffrey Chaucer sets thirty pilgrims on the road from a Southwark inn to Becket's shrine at Canterbury, hands them a game (each tells a tale, the best wins supper), and then does the thing no one had done in English: he lets every sort of person speak as fully themselves. The Wife of Bath, five times married, talks for eight hundred lines before she deigns to begin her story, arguing and flirting and refusing to be ashamed of any of it. The Pardoner hawks pig bones as the relics of saints, thunders a sermon against greed, and knows precisely what he is. No tale can be peeled from its teller; each story is a confession the speaker never means to make. The whole muddy road becomes England talking to itself, bawdy and holy and gloriously alive, in the language we still speak.

title: The Year of the Death of Ricardo Reis
author: José Saramago
day: Ricardo Reis arrives in Lisbon; Saramago opening
extract: We are the dreams of a god who chose not to believe in us.
blurb: Here the sea ends and the land begins, and it is raining over the colourless city as a ship carries Ricardo Reis home to Lisbon. He has come to mourn Fernando Pessoa, the poet who invented him, dead these few weeks; and the dead man returns the visit, climbing the hotel stairs through the months the newly dead are allowed to linger, sitting to talk and growing fainter with each call, while the heteronym he once dreamed up goes on breathing. Saramago holds this vertigo perfectly level and lets the question of which man is the more real come quietly loose in your hands. Around them Salazar's Lisbon hardens and the Spanish war begins to bleed across the border, until Reis's lovely Horatian creed of accepting fate without grief shows itself as something only a poem can afford. The prose runs on like a slow river, weather and thought and unmarked speech poured into one current, and the pull of it is the whole pleasure: stop fighting and drift.

title: In Memoriam A.H.H.
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
extract: 'Tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
blurb: Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky. One section is set on a New Year's Eve, the bells carrying across the midnight snow as Tennyson asks them to ring out the grief that saps the mind. In Memoriam A.H.H. is the elegy he kept writing for seventeen years after Arthur Henry Hallam, the dearest friend of his youth, died without warning in Vienna at twenty-two. It runs to 131 sections, each sealed in a four-line stanza whose outer rhymes reach across the inner pair to close, the shape of a hand trying to hold what is no longer there. The years of its making were the years geology was quietly unmaking Victorian faith, and Tennyson refused to look away: nature is red in tooth and claw, and still he asked whether love could outlast what the mind now honestly knew. The famous verdict, that it is better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all, is nothing handed over cheaply here. It was won across seventeen winters, against everything that wanted it to be untrue.
